"﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾"
The discussion of the meanings of their like has already been treated fully at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah.

Know that the spelling out of the letters (al-tahajji), where the purpose is challenge (al-ta'jiz), occurs in many of the surahs of the Qur'an, and it is not necessary that the mention of the Qur'an or the Book follow those letters, although that is the most common pattern in the surahs of the Qur'an, except for three surahs: the opening of Surat Maryam, the opening of this surah, and the opening of Surat al-Rum. Moreover, this surah is not free of an allusion to the challenge of the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is it not enough for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 2:

﴿Do the people think that they will be left alone because they say, "We believe," and they will not be tried?﴾

The interrogative in ﴿Do they think﴾ is used for denial, i.e., denying that they think this. "Hasiba" (حَسِبَ) means "to suppose" (ظَنَّ), and it has been discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214] in Surat al-Baqarah. By "the people" is meant all those who believe, so the saying is a metonymy (كِنَايَة) for the occurrence of what is said in reality. That is, do the people suppose that their being left alone, [in the sense of] their not being made to say "We believe," has occurred? So His saying ﴿that they will be left alone﴾ (أنْ يُتْرَكُوا) is the first object of "hasiba." His saying ﴿that they say, "We believe"﴾ (أنْ يَقُولُوا آمَنّا) is a clausal phrase in the place of the second object, and it is in the genitive with an elided particle of genitive, the lam of causation (لام التَّعْلِيل), with "an" (أنْ) elided in a regular manner. The implied meaning is: Do the people suppose that their being left alone, not being tried, is for the sake of their saying, "We believe"? For verbs of supposition and knowledge do not take objects that are essences (الذَّوَاتِ); they take states (الأحْوالِ) and meanings (المَعانِي). Their proper form would be that their object is a single term indicating a state. However, usage has settled on making a noun of essence the object, then making what indicates a state of that essence a second object. For this reason, they said that the two objects of the verbs of the heart, i.e., knowledge and the like, originally are a subject and predicate (مُبْتَدَأٌ وخَبَرٌ).

"Tark" (التَّرْك) is leaving something without attending to it after being in contact with it.

Here "tark" is used in its literal sense, because those who believed had been mixing with the polytheists and were among their company. When they believed, they separated themselves and differed from the conditions of their people. That is a likely reason for the polytheists to leave them and their affairs. When the polytheists refused except to contend with them, hoping to turn them away from faith, this came upon them as a surprise and cause for wonder. The figurative "tark" was discussed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He left them in darkness, not seeing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17] at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

﴿That they say﴾ (أنْ يَقُولُوا) is in the place of the accusative, with the removal of the genitive particle, which is the lam of causation; the implied meaning is: for the sake of ﴿that they say, "We believe."﴾

The clause ﴿and they will not be tried﴾ is a circumstantial clause (حال), i.e., they do not suppose that they are safe from trial when they believe.

"Al-Fitan" and "al-Futun" (الفِتَنُ والفُتُونُ) mean the corruption of people's condition through aggression and harm to their selves, their wealth and their families. The noun is "fitna" (الفِتْنَة), and it was discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The verbs ﴿are left﴾ (يُتْرَكُوا) and ﴿will be tried﴾ (يُفْتَنُونَ) are in the passive voice, to dispense with mentioning the agent, because it is clear that the agent is a people who are not believers. That is, they are left free from the trials of the disbelievers against them, owing to what is known of the events just before its revelation, and what is known of the habit of people to show enmity toward those who oppose their beliefs and who hold themselves aloof from their vices. The meaning: Do those who said "We believe" suppose that the enemies of the religion will leave them without trying them? As for those who interpreted "futun" here as including arduous obligations such as emigration and jihad, they have strayed from the clear path of meaning and wording, and they have contradicted what follows from His saying: ﴿So Allah will surely make known those who are truthful, and He will surely make known the liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3].

We did not take the subject of ﴿are left﴾ and ﴿will be tried﴾ to be Allah, exalted is He, out of avoidance of resemblance, while there is an alternative to it.

These trials have degrees, the greatest of which is torture, as was done to Bilal, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, and his parents.

[Page 204]

This is a transition to highlighting trials for the sake of faith in God, showing that it is God's custom (sunnah) with the believers of earlier times. The sentence is emphasized with the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and the particle of certainty (harf al-tahqiq), to set down the believers' state when they considered what they suffered from the polytheists to be too great and were slow to receive victory over the wrongdoers, and when they were heedless of the custom of creation in that situation. It treats them as one who denies that whoever opposes the masses in their error and distances himself from their morals and baseness is bound to be afflicted with a trial from them.

Since this custom is one of the effects of what God has imprinted on the minds of most humans and on their thinking, which is not protected by proofs, and since it occurred among all the earlier nations, God's name is attached to the trials of those nations by a figurative attribution (isnad majazi), because He is the Creator of their causes, just as He created the causes of protection for whoever is worthy of protection from the like of it. This attribution also implies that the One who created the causes of those trials, near and far, is able to avert them by causes that oppose them. Moses' supplication, related in Surah Yunus, points to this: ﴿And Moses said, "Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world. Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment."﴾ [Yunus: 88]. So he asked God to create the opposite of the causes that deceived Pharaoh and his chiefs and covered his heart with error.

The purpose is to remind the believers of what befell the righteous of earlier nations of harm and persecution, as the righteous among the Christians suffered from the Roman polytheists in the early ages of Christianity. The Qur'an has related some of that in "Surah al-Buruj".

Its ruling applies to the situation of everyone who holds fast to the truth among a people who make light of it, even among Muslims, because denial of the truth takes many forms.

The waw that enters upon the sentence ﴿And We certainly tested those before them﴾ may be a conjunction with the sentence "Do the people think..." It may also be a conjunction with the sentence "while they will not be tested", so that it has the sense of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "while indeed We tested those before them." On either reading the sentence is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between what precedes it and what follows from His words ﴿so God will certainly know those who are truthful﴾. So you may call that waw parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah). The attribution of the verb "tested" to God, Exalted, is to honor these trials, in that they proceed according to God's custom with the nations. The fa' in His words ﴿so God will certainly know those who are truthful﴾ is a consequence of the sentence ﴿while they will not be tested﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2], meaning: they will be tested, so God will know those among them who are truthful and those who are liars. What is consequent is God's knowledge that comes about in the future, as the emphasis of the verb of knowing with the energetic nun requires, since the energetic nun is attached to the present tense only for the future. This is a connection to the object of knowledge, resembling the actual (tanjizi) connection of the attributes of will and power, even though they did not name it by this name.

The meaning of truthfulness here is the firmness and steadfastness of a thing, and the meaning of lying is its loss and instability. That is because when the believers said "We believe," none of them was lying in reporting about himself that he held the creed of faith and followed His Messenger. When trial befell them because they entered the religion of Islam, whoever did not care about that and did not abandon following the Messenger has shown the firmness of his faith and the steadiness of his resolve, so his faith was true and sincere. Whoever abandoned faith out of fear of trial has shown from his state the lack of firmness of his faith and its instability. This is like the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Those are a people whose valor is never false"

and the saying of al-A'sha describing the opposite, about his riding camel:

"A she-camel of the breed of camels, that bounds in the heat when the sinning noons lie"

This has already been discussed at His words, exalted is He, ﴿that for them is a sure footing with their Lord﴾ [Yunus: 2] at the beginning of Surah Yunus.

Since God's knowledge of whose faith will be truthful at the time of trial, and whose faith will be false in these two senses, was established in eternity before the trial and the truth and falsehood occurred, it is necessary to interpret the verb "will know" (fa-la-ya'lamanna) as meaning: "will know the falsity of their faith" in this sense. So it is a connection of knowledge to the occurrence of a matter that was in God's knowledge that it would happen. This resembles the connection of will expressed as the actual connection (al-ta'alluq al-tanjizi). There is no objection to affirming two connections for God's knowledge: one eternal, and the other actual and newly occurring. This does not lead to God being described by a newly occurring attribute, because the connection of an attribute is the realization of its requirement in external reality, not in the essence of the thing it describes. This was discussed at His words, exalted is He, ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surah al-Baqarah, and at His words ﴿and that God may know those who believe and take martyrs from among you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140] in Al 'Imran.

You may also make knowledge here a metonymy (kinayah) for the promise to the truthful and the threat to the liars, because knowledge is a cause of recompense according to what it requires. So the metonymy is intended, and it is the more important meaning.

In His words ﴿so God will certainly know﴾ he shifted from the first person of speech to the third person of absence by mentioning the name of majesty (ism al-jalalah), by way of the device of shifting (iltifat), because of the majesty in this mention, so that it is known that the recompense for that is the recompense of the Owner of the kingdom.

The definition of those who are characterized by sincere faith by the relative pronoun and the past-tense relative clause is to convey that they became known for the recent origin of sincere faith, and that their sincerity is established.

As for the definition of those characterized by lying by means of the definite article and the active participle form, it is to convey that they were known for this description and distinguished by it, along with what this carries of variety of expression and observance of the rhyme (fasilah).

Al-Tabari related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: This verse, "Alif Lam Mim. Do the people think that they will be left..." [al-'Ankabut: 1-2], down to His words "and He will certainly know the liars," was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir when he was being tortured for God's sake, and similar to him 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn al-Walid, and Salamah ibn Hisham, of those who were being tortured in Mecca. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to ask God to save them and the oppressed believers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 4:

﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they will outrun Us? Evil is what they judge.﴾

The affirmation of the believers' steadfastness in the face of the persecution they suffer from the polytheists, and the promise and warning contained in that, were followed by a rebuke to the polytheists for the evil deeds they commit against the believers. The greatest of those evil deeds is their persecution of the Muslims. Thus, by "those who commit evil deeds" is meant those who persecute the believers.

This also contains a warning to them that God will not let them escape. In this there is also further affirmation for the believers that God will give them victory over their enemies.

Here "am" (أم) is used for the transitional turning away (al-idrab al-intiqali), and after it an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari) is to be understood.

The "evil deeds" (al-sayyi'at) are the bad actions, namely the punishing, the torture, and the persecution of the Muslims.

Al-sabq (outrunning) is used figuratively for escape and getting away, as in the verse of Murra ibn 'Adda al-FaqImSi:

Page 207

"As though you had never been outrun by fate even once, when you reach what you were seeking."

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We are not to be outrun in replacing your likes﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 60], and His saying: ﴿So they were arrogant in the earth and they were not outrunners﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 39], ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 40].

This was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that they have outrun﴾ [al-Anfal: 59], in surat al-Anfal. The meaning is: "Or do they think that they have cooled their rage against the believers, and so have prevailed over Our allies, and thereby have overcome Us!"

The clause ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾ is a censure of their supposing that, and a nullification of it. It therefore confirms the meaning of denial in the clause ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think﴾, and so it has the force of emphasis, which is why it is detached (without a conjunction).

This clause requires that this supposition was actually held by them. Its occurrence means that they held a belief equivalent to this supposition, because when the believers were unable to repel their trials, they were deceived into thinking that they had overcome the believers. Since the believers were calling to God rather than to the idols, whoever overcomes them has thought that he has overcome the one to whom they call. They are not aware of this supposition, so understand it.

The word "judge" (yahkumun) is used in the sense of conjecture and belief, mocking them for having set themselves in the position of one who judges and is obeyed. "What they judge" is a relative construction with its relative clause; that is, "evil is the judgment they make."

Although this verse was revealed concerning the polytheists who harmed the believers, it alludes to a warning to the Muslims against resembling them in committing evil deeds, treating God's threat against them lightly; for in doing so they take on something of the resemblance of the supposition of escape, even though the believer does not think this, but he is treated as one who thinks it, because of his turning away from the threat at the moment he commits the evil deed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 5:

﴿Whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah, then indeed the term of Allah is surely coming, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

This is addressed specifically to the believers, because they are the ones who hope for the meeting with Allah. The sentence thus serves to state explicitly what His saying ﴿that they will outrun us﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 4] alluded to, namely the promise of victory for the believers over their enemy.

Page 208

It explains it; for this reason it is separated (fusilat) from what precedes it. Had it not been for this close relation, the proper way to state it would have been with a conjunction particle. "Hoping for the meeting with Allah" means the expectation that one will certainly be brought forward for the reckoning of Allah.

"The meeting with Allah" means the gathering (al-hashr) for recompense, because people receive the address of Allah concerning them, whether for them or against them, directly and without intermediary. This has already been discussed in His saying ﴿those who assume that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46] and His saying ﴿and know that you will meet Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The "term of Allah" (ajal Allah) may be the time that Allah has determined in His knowledge for the resurrection and the reckoning. In that case it is an instance of putting the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun (al-izhar fi maqam al-idmar). The apparent form would have required saying "fa-innahu la-ati", but he turned to the apparent noun, as in the attribution of "ajal" to the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalala), which indicates that it cannot be broken. The intent is to stress exhortation toward preparedness.

It may also be that the intended meaning of "ajal Allah" is the term that Allah has appointed for the victory of the believers and the ending of the trial the polytheists inflict upon them, through the eradication of the instigators of that trial, who are the chieftains of Quraysh. This happened through the victory at the Battle of Badr and what followed it, up to the conquest of Mecca. In that case the speech is a confirmation for the Messenger ﷺ and the believers when the believers had become impatient for victory to free them from the trial of the polytheists, so that they might worship Allah without being tormented in their worship. The meaning on this reading is: if you believe in the resurrection with a certainty that springs from affirming Allah's promise of it, then your affirmation of the coming of victory is more fitting, since He has promised it to you. So "man" is conditional, and the verb of the condition is made the verb "to be" (kana), to indicate that this hope is firmly established in the agent of the conditional verb.

For this reason, His saying ﴿the term of Allah is surely coming﴾ is the answer to His saying ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah﴾, by considering its indication of an implied answer, so that the connection between the meaning of the conditional clause and the meaning of the consequent clause is maintained. Were it not so, the connection between the condition and the consequence would break down, since it would lead to the meaning: "whoever does not hope for the meeting with Allah, then the term of Allah is not coming," and this does not fit the course of speech. Therefore it is necessary to posit something implied by way of implicative indication (dalalat al-iqtida').

The emphasis on the consequent clause with a particle of emphasis, on the first reading, serves exhortation and urging toward preparation for the meeting with Allah; on the second reading, it serves to establish the promised victory, treating their impatience as if it were hesitation, in order to kindle their certainty in what Allah has promised, so that the lengthening of the period, which the waiting magnifies, does not weaken them. By this the effect of the concluding phrase becomes apparent, with the two attributes "the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing" rather than other exalted attributes. The attribute "All-Hearing" alludes to the fact that Allah heard the words of some of them in supplication for the hastening of victory, as His exalted saying indicates: ﴿and they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the victory of Allah?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], and like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ:

"O Allah, deliver 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah. O Allah, deliver al-Walid ibn al-Walid. O Allah, deliver Salamah ibn Hisham. O Allah, deliver the oppressed among the believers. O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar. O Allah, make it upon them as the years of Joseph."

The allusion through the attribute "All-Knowing" is to the fact that Allah knows what is in their souls of haste for victory. Had the intended meaning of "ajal Allah" been death, there would be no point in informing of its coming, let alone emphasizing it; likewise, had the intended meaning been the resurrection, His saying ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah﴾ would have been sufficient. This is the sense of what the verses indicate through explicit statement and implication. Turning them away from this course and toward what is found in al-Kashshaf and Mafatih al-Ghayb, taken from the words of Abu 'Ubaydah, is a diversion of them from their proper path and a turning of the word "hope" from its meaning, and a dislocation of the composition of the speech from its being one part holding to the joints of another.

The apparent noun "Allah" in the phrase ﴿fa-inna ajal Allah la-ati﴾, although the apparent form would require the pronoun, is due to the prior mention of the Name of Allah in the conditional clause ﴿whoever hopes for the meeting with Allah﴾; this is so that the reference of the pronoun does not become ambiguous by being returned to "man," since the intended meaning is to inform of a specific term, namely the time of the promised victory, as in His saying: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Saba': 29] ﴿Say, "For you is an appointment of a day from which you will not delay an hour, nor will you advance."﴾ [Saba': 30]

He expressed by the verb of hope the anticipation of the resurrection, because the speech is addressed to the believers, and they are among those who hope for the meeting with Allah, since they await the resurrection for the good things they hope for in it. Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, said when he was dying, quoting the verse of one of the Ash'aris who had come as a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ:

"Tomorrow I shall meet the beloved, Muhammad and his companions."

**[Page 210]**

That is, "and whoever strives [among] those who hope for the meeting with Allah." The *waw* here is not one of division (*taqsim*), and the one who strives is not a separate category from those who hope for the meeting with Allah. Rather, striving is one of the attributes of those who hope for the meeting with Allah.

*Jihad* (striving, exerting oneself in the way of Allah) is an intensive form of *jahd*, which is the verbal noun of *jahada* (in the pattern of *manaʿa*), meaning that one exerts himself in his work and takes on hardship in it. For this reason, its use became common for fighting in defense of Islam. Here it may refer to enduring the hardships and harms inflicted upon the Muslims for the sake of their entry into Islam and their rejection of the religion of polytheism, when the polytheists confronted them with harm. Thus the use of *jihad* here is like its use in His statement, exalted is He, after this: ﴿And if they strive to make you associate with Me [something] of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut 29:8], and like its use in the statement of the Prophet ﷺ when he returned from one of his expeditions: "We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad."

This sense is the most evident in this surah, on the basis that it is entirely Meccan, since fighting-jihad did not take place in Mecca.

The meaning of ﴿Then he strives only for himself﴾ on this interpretation is that the hardships he encounters are for the benefit of his own self, so that he may remain steadfast in the faith, by which he is saved from punishment in the Hereafter.

It is also permissible that *jihad* be understood in the sense it acquired in the technical terminology of the Sharia, namely fighting the disbelievers for the sake of supporting Islam and defending its territory. In that case, its mention here serves to prepare the souls of the Muslims for what they will have to resort to, namely fighting the polytheists, before they are compelled to it. This is like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Say to the bedouins who were left behind: "You will be called to a people of great might; you will fight them, or they will submit."﴾ [al-Fath 48:16]. The reason for alluding to this sense is that His statement ﴿Indeed, the term of Allah is coming﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut 29:5] implied an expectation of the promise of their victory over their enemy, so He preceded this by informing them that it would come after a severe struggle, and that is what occurred at the Battle of Badr.

The meaning of ﴿Then he strives only for himself﴾ on this interpretation is the same as its meaning in the first interpretation, because that jihad repels the polytheists' obstruction of them from Islam, so continued adherence to Islam depends upon it. There is also an additional meaning: that this jihad, although it is outwardly a defense of the religion of Allah, is also by it their victory, the safety of the lives of the living among them, their families and their children, and the foundation of their authority on earth. As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds that He will surely grant them succession upon the earth, as He granted it to those before them, and that He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and will surely change their state, after their fear, to security﴾ [al-Nur 24:55]. ʿAlqama ibn Shayban al-Tamimi said:

*We fight the enemies on behalf of our sons, and upon our insight, even if we do not see.*

The more fitting option, in terms of the eloquence of the Qur'an, is that both interpretations are intended, as we mentioned in the ninth introduction among the introductions to this commentary.

The restriction (*qasr*) derived from *innama* ("only") is the restriction of striving to being for the sake of the striver's own self, that is, for the benefit of the striver himself, since the cause (*ʿilla*) does not relate to the self but to its states. That is: striving for the benefit of his own self, not for a benefit that returns to Allah, exalted is He. The restriction produced by the particle *innama* is therefore a figurative restriction (*qasr iddiʿaʾi*), intended to draw attention to the benefits that accrue to the souls of the strivers, which they overlook when they strive in both of its senses. For this reason, the restriction's implied rejection is followed by its justification: that Allah is free of need from the worlds, so nothing of the jihad is for Allah, exalted is He, but its benefit is for the community.

Thus the position of the emphatic particle here is the position of the *fa* of consequence (*fa* of *tafriʿ*), which the author of *Dalaʾil al-Iʿjaz* (ʿAbd al-Qahir al-Jurjani) pointed out, and which has been discussed more than once before.

It is permissible that this is a conjunction (ʿatf, coordination) with the clause ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that they can outrun Us?﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 4], because of the threat and warning contained in the clause it is joined to. So there is joined to it what is a promise and good news for those who believed and did righteous deeds, together with what led to mention of this promise in the preceding saying of Allah: ﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 6]. The content of the clause ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ to the end of the verse explains the nature of the striving of the one who strives for himself.

It is also permissible that it is a conjunction with the clause ﴿And whoever strives, he strives only for himself﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 6]. The conjunction is used in view of what the relative pronoun and its relative clause point to, namely that the cause of this good reward is that they believed and did righteous deeds. The phrase is expressed in the form of a noun (ism zāhir) in place of a pronoun (ḍamīr), for the purpose of this indication.

Page 212

The reward is a bounty (faḍl), because when a servant complies with the command of Allah, he has only averted from himself the consequence of disobedience. As for the reward for obeying one's Master, that is a bounty from the Master. The forgiveness of their previous evil deeds is a great bounty, because they deserved to be held accountable for what they had done, and their desisting from that in the future does not require overlooking the past. Yet this is an addition to the bounty.

"Aḥsan" (best) is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), which is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, a cognate object) of the verb in "la-najziyannahum" (we shall surely reward them). The sense is: "and We shall surely reward them with a reward that is best."

Its being annexed to ﴿that which they used to do﴾ serves to convey the greatness of the entire reward. Thus it is estimated as the best of their deeds. The sense of the statement is: "We shall surely reward them for all their righteous deeds with a reward equal to the best of their righteous deeds." This includes those who, after the revelation of this verse, were polytheists and then believed and did righteous deeds.

[p. 213]

﴿We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. But if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, then do not obey them. To Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾ ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds - We will surely admit them among the righteous.﴾

The Qur'an has not left unaddressed any of the circumstances of the relationships between Muslims and polytheists without specifying the obligation that befits their faith in each of them. Among the strongest of these relationships is the bond of kinship. Kinship between a polytheist and a believer calls for kindness and good companionship, but difference of religion calls for hostility and resentment, especially when the polytheists were firmly set in their polytheism and fearful that the call of Islam would come upon the basis of their religion. They would therefore harm the Muslims so that they might abandon following Islam. Through this verse, God clarified what is incumbent upon the Muslim in dealing with his polytheist relatives. He singled out from among them the kinship of the parents because it is the closest kinship, so that whatever is less than it would be more appropriate for the ruling that is legislated for it.

An incident, or two incidents, occurred that prompted the detailing of this ruling. It was narrated that when Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas [may Allah be pleased with him] embraced Islam, his mother Hamnah bint Abi Sufyan said to him: "O Sa'd, I have heard that you have turned away from your religion. It was also narrated that when Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Makhzumi embraced Islam and emigrated with 'Umar ibn al-Khattab to Madinah before the emigration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Jahl and his brother al-Harith, who were the maternal brothers of Ayyash, went out. They approached Ayyash and said to him: "Muhammad commands kindness to parents, and you have abandoned your mother. She has sworn that she will neither eat nor drink nor shelter in any house until she sees you. She loves you more than she loves us, so come out with us." He consulted 'Umar, and 'Umar said: "They are deceiving you." But they kept at him until he disregarded 'Umar's advice and went out with them. When they reached al-Bayda', Abu Jahl said: "My camel has become exhausted, so carry me with you." Ayyash said: "Yes." He dismounted to make his mount kneel for himself and for Abu Jahl, and they seized him, bound him tightly, and took him to his mother. She said to him: "You will remain in torment until you turn away from the religion of Muhammad." She kept him bound with her. It was said that this verse was revealed concerning the matter of these two.

The purpose of the verse is His saying: ﴿But if they strive to make you associate with Me﴾ to the end of it. It was opened with ﴿We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾ because it serves as an introduction to the purpose, so that it is known that the enjoining of kindness to parents does not require obeying them in evil and the like, in accordance with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no obedience to a created being in disobedience to the Creator." Also, the purpose is to establish the ruling of kindness to parents in every situation except the situation of associating partners with God, so that it does not become unclear to the Muslims how to reconcile the command to be kind to parents with the command to disobey them if they command polytheism. This also serves to refute the saying of Abu Jahl: "Is not kindness to parents part of the religion of Muhammad?" and similar statements.

This is one of the methods of disputation, which is called al-qawl bil-muwjib ("accepting the premise"): granting the argument while the dispute remains. An example of it in the Qur'an is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "You are only human beings like us. You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship, so bring us a clear authority."﴾ [Ibrahim: 10] ﴿Their messengers said to them: "We are only human beings like you, but Allah bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants."﴾ [Ibrahim: 11] Thus it is known that there is no contradiction between kindness to parents and disregarding their command in matters that do not relate to their own affairs.

Tawsiyah ("enjoining") is like iya' (commissioning); one says awsa and wassa. It is a command to do something in the absence of the one who commands it, so the idea of exhortation to the commanded act is contained within iya'. This was mentioned in His saying: ﴿The bequest to parents﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and in His saying, "And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons," in al-Baqarah.

The verb wisayah transitively reaches the one enjoined by means of the preposition bi-, as you say: awsa bi-abna'ihi ila fulan, meaning he enjoined concerning his children's affairs to so-and-so. It also transitively reaches the act commanded by means of bi-, which is the original usage, as in "And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons." When one combines the one enjoined and the thing enjoined, and the deletion of the preposition from the substitute is common, relying on its presence in the substituted element, then His saying here, "We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents," is similar. Its implied meaning is: "We have enjoined upon man concerning his parents with kindness," with the preposition omitted (naz' al-khafid).

Husn ("kindness") is an infinitive noun, meaning bi-ihsan ("with goodness"). The clause ﴿But if they strive to make you associate with Me﴾ is conjoined to the clause "We have enjoined," and it implies an omitted verb of speech, because the preceding clause carries the meaning of speech.

Mujahadah means exerting maximal effort in an act, that is, insisting earnestly so that you associate with Me.

By knowledge in His saying ﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾ is meant true knowledge grounded in evidence of reason or revelation. That is, that you associate with Me things for which you find in yourself no proof of their deserving worship, as in His saying: "﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾" [Hud: 46], meaning knowledge of the possibility of its existence. In al-Kashshaf it is said that the negation of knowledge is a kinaya (implicature) for the negation of the known object, as if He said: that you associate with Me something that cannot validly be a god, that is, that cannot validly be known. He means that it belongs to the category of their saying "this is nothing," as he expressly stated in his commentary on Surat Luqman, as in His saying: ﴿What they call upon besides Him is falsehood﴾ [Luqman: 30].

The clause ﴿To Me is your return﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf bayani, an explanatory resumption) to further confirm what the introductory part of the verse, His saying ﴿We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾, had indicated. Since the rest of the verse signaled the gravity of the matter of polytheism and warned against obeying a person's parents in it, this would stir a question in the minds of the children: whether they should treat their parents harshly because of their association of partners. They were informed that the punishment of their parents for polytheism is entrusted to Allah, exalted is He, for it is He who rewards the good-doers and the wrong-doers.

Al-marji' ("the return") means the resurrection. Al-inba' ("informing") means informing, and it is used as a kinaya for His knowledge, exalted is He, of what they do, both outward and hidden deeds, that is, what they conceal from the Muslims and what they harbour in their hearts. This is also a kinaya for the requital for it, whether good or evil. Thus in His saying ﴿and I will inform you﴾ there are two kinayat: the first is an allusion (iima'), and the second is an insinuation (talwih). That is: I will repay you with reward for your disobedience to them in what they command, and I will repay them with punishment for their association of partners.

The clause ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds - We will surely admit them among the righteous﴾ is an explicit statement of some of what the kinaya in His saying ﴿and I will inform you of what you used to do﴾ implied, giving attention to the aspect of the reward of the believers. The nobility of this reward has been indicated by its being the reward of the perfectly righteous, as in His saying: "﴿Those will be with those whom Allah has blessed of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾" [al-Nisa': 69]. Do you not see the saying of Sulayman: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml: 19]?

So Allah made as a recompense for the loneliness of that separation companionship, by placing him among the righteous, with whom he finds comfort.

This is a group from among those who embraced Islam in Mecca. Their condition in their dealings with the polytheists was that of one who cannot endure harm. When harm reached them, they returned to polytheism in their hearts and concealed this from the Muslims, and so they became hypocrites (munafiqun). Allah revealed this verse concerning them before the Hijra. This was said by al-Dahhak and Jabir ibn Zayd. It has already been mentioned at the end of Surah al-Nahl that among these were al-Harith ibn Rabi'a ibn al-Aswad, Abu Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Ali ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf, and al-'As ibn Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj. These people were lured down by Satan, and they reverted to disbelief in their hearts, because their faith was weak. The harm that befell them was the cause of their apostasy. Yet they began to show the Muslims that they were with them. It is likely that this display was by agreement between them and the polytheists: they were content that they would mix with the Muslims in order to bring the polytheists news of the Muslims. Allah therefore counted them as hypocrites and threatened them with this verse.

The words of His, exalted is He, ﴿Among people is he who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ point to the fact that the faith of these people had not taken firm root in their hearts. His words ﴿he regards the trial of people as like the punishment of Allah﴾ point to the fact that this group is punished with the punishment of Allah. His words ﴿So Allah will surely make evident those who believed, and He will surely make evident the hypocrites﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 11] point to the fact that they are hypocrites who conceal disbelief. Therefore, it is certain that they are among the group concerning whom Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath from Allah﴾ [al-Nahl: 106], and that they are other than the group whom Allah, exalted is He, excepted with His words: ﴿except one who has been forced while his heart remains firm in faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106]. Thus there is no contradiction between this verse and the verses at the end of Surah al-Nahl, as might be supposed from the silence of the exegetes about explaining the rulings derived from this verse, while they mention the rulings derived from the verses of Surah al-Nahl.

The particle of location in His words ﴿harmed for Allah's sake﴾ is used with the meaning of causation, like the particle lam. That is, "he was harmed on account of Allah," i.e., on account of following what Allah called him to.

His words ﴿he regards the trial of people as like the punishment of Allah﴾ mean making it equal to the punishment of Allah, as required by the basic principle of comparison. Thus, if these people believed in resurrection and recompense, the meaning of this making is that they equated the punishment of this world with the punishment of the Hereafter, as is the apparent sense of the comparison. So they guarded against the trial of people and neglected the side of the punishment of Allah and did not care for it, giving precedence to what is immediate and discarding what is deferred. The more fitting course for them would have been to make the punishment of Allah greater than the harm of people. And if they had discarded belief in resurrection as a consequence of discarding faith, then the meaning of "making" is that they made it like the punishment of Allah in the eyes of the believers who believe in recompense.

Thus the statement from His words ﴿Among people﴾ to His words ﴿like the punishment of Allah﴾ is an allusion to blame and to foolishness, on both possible interpretations, although the degree of blame varies.

Allah, exalted is He, clarified their intention in displaying Islam: they made the display of Islam a provision against the victory of the Muslims that might be expected in the future, so that they would find themselves exposed to the benefits of that victory. This indicates that this verse was revealed shortly before the Hijra from Mecca, when people were entering Islam and its affairs were increasing.

The emphasis of the conditional clause in His words ﴿And if victory comes from your Lord, they will surely say﴾ is by the lam that prepares for an oath, to affirm that the answer will occur when the condition occurs. It requires affirming that both matters will certainly happen. Thus there is a promise in it that Allah, exalted is He, is the helper of the Muslims, and that the hypocrites will say that at that time. It is likely that this took place on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, and whoever of this group was alive said it, desiring thereby to attain the rank of precedence in Islam. The historians mentioned that al-Aqra' ibn Habis, 'Uyayna ibn Hisn, Suhayl ibn 'Amr, and a group of the notables of the Arabs were at the door of 'Umar, waiting for permission to enter. Bilal, Salman, and 'Ammar ibn Yasir were at the door. 'Umar's permission went out for Salman, Bilal, and 'Ammar to enter, and the faces of the rest changed. Suhayl ibn 'Amr said to them: "Do not let your faces change. They were called and we were called; they hurried and we delayed. If you envy them at the door of 'Umar, then what Allah has prepared for them in Paradise is greater."

His words ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of what is within the breasts of the worlds?﴾ form a concluding statement (tadhyil). The "wa" is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya), and the interrogative is one of denial, denying them their statement ﴿We believe in Allah﴾ and their statement ﴿Indeed, we were with you﴾. This is because they said that out of the supposition that their lie and hypocrisy would pass over the Messenger of Allah. So the denial against them implies that they were lying in their two statements mentioned.

The address is directed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in order that they might hear this address, for they attend the gatherings of the Prophet and the believers, and they listen to what is revealed of the Qur'an and what is recited from it after its revelation. Thus they feel that Allah has knowledge of their inner thoughts.

It is also possible that the interrogative is affirmative (taqriri), in which Allah directed the address to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of affirmation of what Allah has bestowed upon him, namely informing him of the conditions of those who are involved in hypocrisy. This style is common in the affirmative interrogative, and it is often confused with the denial interrogative, and only context distinguishes between them, that is, "So do not believe their speech."

The elative in His words ﴿most knowing﴾ takes into account the knowledge of some Muslims of some of what is in the breasts of these hypocrites, from among those who were given insight and sound judgment. You may also take the elative form as stripped of comparison, that is: "Is not Allah knowing with a detailed knowledge, nothing hidden from Him?"

Two groups were singled out for mention from among those covered by the generality of His words "the worlds", out of concern for these two groups and their conditions: the group of those who believe, and the group of the hypocrites. This is because the knowledge of what is in the breasts of both groups, of faith or hypocrisy, entails the reward appropriate to their conditions in this world and the next, and that is both encouragement and warning.

The reason both verbs are emphasized with the lam of oath (lam al-qasam) and the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid) is that the purpose of this report is to refute the belief of the hypocrites that God does not inform His Messenger of what is in their souls. So the purpose of the two reports is the second of them, I mean His saying: ﴿And He will surely know the hypocrites﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿Allah will surely know those who believe﴾, it is a preface to what follows and an explicit statement that the false faith is not confused with true faith.

In this there is also the intention of the figurative meaning (al-ma'na al-kinai) of knowledge, which is the requital of each group according to what God knows of its condition.

The verb for these two groups is in the present-future form, since the emphatic nun is not used to affirm an affirmative report unless it refers to the future. This is either because knowledge is here a metonymy (kinaya) for its necessary consequence, which is the treatment of each group according to what it deserves based on what is known of its condition, and requital is a future matter; or because what is meant is knowledge of a future matter, namely the variation of their states on the day the victory comes. Thus, perhaps those who were hypocrites at the time the verse was revealed will be believers on the day of victory, and some people will remain upon their hypocrisy.

The difference between the believers and the hypocrites in expression is that the first are described by means of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) and the past-tense relative clause (al-sila al-madiya), while the second are described by means of the definite article (al-lam) and the active participle (ism al-fa'il). This is because the relative pronoun indicates their being well known for faith, and the past-tense verb indicates that faith has taken firm root in them and preceded them, while the definite article indicates that they have become known for hypocrisy and that it came upon them after they had been believers. Thus there is in it a characterization of the evil of their end, along with the variety of expression and observing the rhyme (ri'ayat al-fasila).

[Page 219]

This is another aspect of the interaction between the polytheists and the believers, namely the attempt by the polytheists to turn the Muslims away from their faith by means of trials, through doubt and deception, directed at those whom they could not afflict with harm and torture. This was either because of their (the believers') honour and the fear of their might, as in the case of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, for it is said that this statement was made to him; or because of their numbers, when the Muslims had multiplied and the polytheists had run out of means to prevent people from embracing Islam.

By "those who disbelieved" is meant a group of them: Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and Abu Sufyan ibn Harb (before he embraced Islam). They said to the Muslims, among whom was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: "We will not be raised, neither we nor you. But if that should happen, we will bear your sins for you." They said this out of ignorance and delusion, by which they hoped to dissuade the Muslims from their belief in the Resurrection, imagining that if the Resurrection did occur, they would be in the Hereafter as they had been in this world: people of protection, guarantee, undoing and decision, like the chiefs of the Arabs, who, when they interceded, were interceded for, and when they undertook responsibility, were held to it.

This is like the saying of al-'As ibn Wa'il to Khabbab ibn al-Aratt: "If God raises me, there will certainly be wealth for me, and I will pay you your debt." It is concerning him that the words of the Exalted were revealed: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ [Maryam: 77]. All of this is disputation through falsehood, and it is a method of argument which, if built upon truth, is acceptable, as is attributed to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib in opposition to this:

They claimed, the astrologer and the physician, both, that bodies will not be gathered. I said to you both:

If your saying is true, I will not lose, but if my saying is true, then the loss is upon you both.

God related their statement ﴿and let us bear your sins﴾ in the form of a command with the imperative lam; either because they spoke in this way due to their eloquence, or to convey the emphasis on their undertaking of that burden contained in their statement. The form of their command to themselves to carry is more emphatic than a report about themselves regarding that, and than a conditional or what has its meaning, because a command calls for compliance, so the form of the command indicates the certainty of fulfilling the guarantee.

The conjunctive waw joining the clause ﴿and let us bear﴾ to the clause ﴿follow our way﴾ implies co-occurrence between the content of the two clauses in the command, not simultaneity of occurrence. So the two clauses have the force of a conditional and its response, and the meaning is established by context.

Thus this statement is more indicative of the emphasis on the commitment to bear the burden, if the Muslims follow the way of the polytheists, than if it were said: "If you follow our way, we will bear your sins," in the conditional form, or: "Follow our way, so we will bear your sins," with the causal fa'.

Al-haml (carrying) is a figurative metaphor depicting the state of one who undertakes the burden of another by the state of one who carries another's goods, and it reverts to the meaning of guarantee and surety.

The phrase "your sins" indicates generality, since it is a plural noun in the genitive construction, which is one of the forms of generality.

His saying ﴿and they will not bear anything of their sins﴾ is a refutation of their statement ﴿and let us bear your sins﴾, negating generality in affirmation with generality in negation; because "shay'" (anything) in a negative context conveys generality, being an indefinite noun, and the addition of the particle "min" makes the generality explicit.

The denied bearing is that whose purpose is to remove responsibility from another and to absolve him of his crimes, so it does not contradict the affirmation of another bearing upon them, which is the bearing of accountability for misguidance, in His saying: ﴿And they will surely bear their burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

The lie reported about them is the lie in what their command to themselves required, namely that they would bear the sins of the Muslims as they claimed, and fulfil that as they had done in this world. This is an undoubted lie, because it contradicts reality and their own belief.

For this reason, the clause ﴿Indeed, they are liars﴾ is an apposition of the clause ﴿they will not bear anything of their sins﴾, because the clause ﴿they will not bear anything of their sins﴾ included the failure of their statement ﴿and let us bear your sins﴾ to correspond to reality in any respect, and this implies that its content is an explicit lie. So the content of the clause ﴿Indeed, they are liars﴾ was included in the content of the clause ﴿they will not bear﴾. The content of the second is not identical to the content of the first; rather, the second is more complete in indicating that their lying is established and that it is a characteristic of them in this report and in others. The structure of this clause is like the structure of a verse from the science of rhetoric:

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 16–17:

﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people: Worship Allah and fear Him. That is better for you, if you only knew. ﴾ ﴿You worship only idols instead of Allah, and you invent a lie. Indeed, those whom you worship instead of Allah possess not for you any provision; so seek provision from Allah, and worship Him, and be grateful to Him. To Him you will be returned.﴾

He moves from the account of Noah to the account of Abraham, because of the parallel between Abraham's rescue from the fire and Noah's rescue from the water. In this there is an indication of the greatness of power, since He saved (someone) from water and from fire.

"And Abraham" is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon Noah. The implied sense is: "And We sent Abraham."

"When" (idh) is an adverbial clause attached to the implied "We sent," meaning: at the time when he said to his people, "Worship Allah," etc., and this was the first period of his call. His saying "Worship Allah" implies that they had not been worshippers of Allah at all.

The clause "That is better for you, if you only knew" is a justification for the command to worship Allah. The report is stated concisely in this clause and detailed by His saying: "Indeed, those whom you worship instead of Allah possess not for you any provision," and so on.

The meaning of "if you only knew" is: if you knew the proofs of Allah's exclusivity in divinity. The object of "knew" is omitted, since what precedes it indicates it. It is also permissible to make the verb "you know" function as intransitive, meaning: if you were people of knowledge and reflection.

The clause "You worship only idols instead of Allah" is a justification for the clause "Worship Allah." Restricting them to worshipping idols may be a restriction to their worshipping idols, meaning instead of worshipping Allah. In that case it is a real restriction (qaṣr ḥaqīqī), since the people of Abraham did not worship Allah. The restriction then bears upon "instead of Allah," meaning: you worship only other than Allah. Accordingly, "instead of Allah" is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from "idols," meaning: in a state of being worshipped instead of Allah. This is the counterpart of His saying "Worship Allah," without his saying to them: "Do not worship except Allah." However, the people of Abraham were described with polytheism in His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat al-An'am: "He said: O my people, I am free from what you associate" [al-An'am: 78]. So they were like the polytheists of the Arabs, and the restriction bears upon their worship, which is characterized by idolatry, meaning: you worship only images that have no perception, so it is a restriction of reversal (qaṣr qalb) to nullify their belief in the divinity of those images, as He said, may He be exalted: "He said: Do you worship what you carve?" [al-Saffat: 95].

Upon both of these two readings, the meaning of His saying "instead of Allah" is explained: "dūn" may be in the sense of "other than (ghayr)," in which case "min" is superfluous, and the meaning is: you worship idols other than Allah. It is also permissible that the word "dūn" be a noun for a distant place, and then it is metaphorically used for the sense of opposition, in which case "min" is for origin (ibtidāʾiyya), and the meaning is: you worship idols described as being opposed to the attributes of Allah.

"Awthān" is the plural of wathan (with two fatḥas), which is an image of stone or wood, fashioned in the form of a human or an animal. The wathan is more specific than the ṣanam, because ṣanam is applied to stones that are not shaped into images, like most of the idols of the Arabs, such as the ṣanam of Dhu al-Khalasa for Khath'am. The idols of the people of Abraham were images, as He said: "He said: Do you worship what you carve?" [al-Saffat: 95]. Their idols' description has already been mentioned in Surat al-Anbiya'.

"Takhluqūn" is the present tense of khalaqa al-khabar, meaning ikhtalaqahu, that is, he fabricated it, i.e., he lied about it and invented it, meaning: you attribute to them reports, virtues and deeds that are false and imagined.

"Ifk" means lying, and it was mentioned in His saying: "Indeed, those who brought the slander are a group among you" [al-Nur: 11] in Surat al-Nur.

As for the clause "Indeed, those whom you worship instead of Allah possess not for you any provision": if the people of Abraham acknowledged to Allah, exalted is He, divinity, creation and provision, but they made for Him partners in worship so that these would be intercessors for them, like the situation of the polytheists of the Arabs, then the clause is a justification for "Worship Allah and fear Him," meaning: He is the one deserving of the worship which is gratitude for His blessings. But if his people did not affirm divinity for anyone other than their idols, then the clause "Indeed, those whom you worship instead of Allah" is a resumed, initiatory sentence, nullifying their belief that their gods provide for them. This possibility is supported by the consequential particle in His saying: "So seek provision from Allah." The hesitation regarding the state of Abraham's people in associating partners was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Shu'ara', and likewise in Surat al-Anbiya'.

The indefiniteness of "provision" (rizq) in a negative context indicates the generality of the negation of the power of their idols over every provision, even a little. The consequence of the command to seek provision from Allah is a nullification of their assumption that provision comes from their idols,

or a reminder that the Provider is Allah, so seeking provision from Him requires singling Him out for worship, as indicated by the conjunction "and worship Him and be grateful to Him." Abraham followed the method of inference from sensory blessings, because establishing them is closer to the minds of the common people.

"ʿInda" is a noun of place, and it is used metaphorically. He likened seeking provision from Allah to searching for something in a place specific to it, so "ʿinda," which indicates a place specific to what the adverb is attached to, was borrowed for it.

Gratitude (shukr) is transitive with the preposition "lām," following the most common usage in Arabic speech, for the purpose of conveying the meaning of exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ) that the lām carries, i.e., entitlement (istiḥqāq).

The lām of definition in "al-rizq" is the lām of genus (lām al-jins), which conveys comprehensiveness (istighrāq) through the aid of the context, meaning: seek every provision, whether little or much, from Allah alone. The defined noun with the lām of genus is in the force of an indefinite noun, so it is as if it were said: "seek provision from Allah." Therefore, the repetition of the word "provision" in the definite form does not necessitate that it is different from the first; so the rule of the indefinite, that when repeated in definite form it is the same as the first, does not apply here.

The clause "To Him you will be returned" is a justification for the command to worship Him and be grateful to Him, meaning: because He is the one who rewards that with reward, and its opposite with punishment; for to Allah, and not to other than Him, is your return after death. In this is an incorporation (idmāj) of the justification for worship with the affirmation of resurrection.
