Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 18:

﴿And if you deny, then indeed nations before you denied, and upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance.﴾

It is permissible that this sentence be part of the continuing speech of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in that he saw from them signs of denial and so supposed its occurrence; or that their denial of him had already preceded this statement of his, so that the purpose of this sentence is the necessary implication of the report, namely that their denial of him is nothing strange, and so it does not harm him, and they should not think that they can harm him by it and take their revenge upon him, for that has befallen the messengers before him from their peoples. For this reason the reciters unanimously agreed upon reading the verb tukadhdhibu (تُكَذِّبُوا) with the second-person ta' of address, and they did not differ over it as they differed over the reading of His saying: ﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 19], etc.

Page 227

It is also permissible that the sentence be parenthetical (mu'tarida) and the waw be parenthetical (i'tiradiyya), the interjection of this speech between the speech of Ibrahim and the answer of his people. Thus it is a speech directed from the side of Allah, exalted is He, to the polytheists, turning from the third-person absence (al-ghayba) to direct address (al-khitab) in order to register it against them. Its purpose is to explain the benefit of narrating the stories of Nuh and Ibrahim, and that the Messenger ﷺ has an example in the messengers of the nations who came before him, especially Ibrahim, the forefather of the Arabs who are addressed, according to this aspect.

The clause ﴿and upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾ is an announcement to the addressees that their denial does not reach him with anything that would be a means of his being harmed; so if it is from the speech of Ibrahim, then by "the Messenger" is meant Ibrahim, and he took the explicit form (al-izhar) in place of the pronoun (al-idmar) to signal that the title "Messenger" indicates that his duty is to convey clearly and plainly what he was sent with; and if it is from Allah's address to the polytheists of Quraysh, then by "the Messenger" is meant Muhammad ﷺ, and this description became predominant for him in the Qur'an, together with the indication that the title of messengership requires nothing but clear conveyance.

This discourse runs along the two readings mentioned in His saying: ﴿And if you deny﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 18]. It is more likely that this is addressed by God Most High to the polytheists, since the majority read "أوَلَمْ يَرَوْا" (awa lam yaraw, "Have they not seen?") with the third-person *ya'* (yā' al-ghaybah), and there was no parallel to His saying ﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 18]. The occasion for mentioning this is the allusion to resurrection in His saying ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245], drawing an analogy between the state of the Arab polytheists and the state of the people of Ibrahim (Abraham).

The majority read "أوَلَمْ يَرَوْا" with the third-person *ya'*, and the pronoun refers to ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 12] in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 12], or to something known from the context of the discourse. On the view that His saying ﴿And if you deny﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 18] etc. is outside the statement of Ibrahim, the third-person pronoun in ﴿Have they not seen?﴾ is an *iltifat* (shift of address, *iltifat*). The shift from address (*khitab*) to the third person serves the purpose of distancing them from the honour of being addressed, after informing about them that they are deniers.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr (from 'Asim), and Khalaf read "أوَلَمْ تَرَوْا" (awa lam taraw, "Have you not seen?") with the second-person *ta'* (tā' al-fawqiyyah), in the manner of ﴿And if you deny﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 18], on the two readings mentioned.

The *hamzah* is the interrogative of denunciation concerning the non-seeing; they are treated as one who has not seen, and so he rebukes them.

The seeing may be visual (*basariyyah*), and reasoning from what is observed of the continual renewal of created things at every moment through birth and the emergence of plants is a clear proof for everyone who has sight.

The *ibda'* of creation is its beginning and bringing into existence after it was not existent. It is said "abda'a" with a *hamzah* at its beginning and "bada'a" without it, and both occur together in this verse: He said ﴿how God originates creation﴾, then He said ﴿So look how He began creation﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 20]. And in His names, Most High, only *al-Mubdi'* (the Originator) has come, not *al-Badi'*.

I think that "abda'a" with a *hamzah* at its beginning is said only when it is coordinated with "yu'idu" (He repeats), but I have not seen anyone restrict it to this.

Al-khalq (creation) is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., *al-makhluq* (the created thing), as in His saying ﴿This is the creation of God, so show me what those other than Him have created﴾ [Luqman: 11].

"Yubdi'" is put in the present form to indicate the continual renewal of the beginning of creation whenever the observer directs his gaze at created things. The sentence ends with His saying ﴿how God originates creation﴾. As for the clause ﴿then He repeats it﴾, it is a fresh, independent (*ibtida'iyyah*) resumption, and it is not governed by the verb "yarawa" (they see), because the repetition of creation after its annihilation is neither visible to them nor do they suppose it. So it is determined that the clause ﴿then He repeats it﴾ is an independent, interposed (*mu'taridah*) sentence between the clause ﴿Have they not seen?﴾ and the clause ﴿Say: Travel through the earth﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 20]. "Thumma" (then) here indicates a graded delay (*tarakhi al-rutbi*), because the matter of the repetition of creation is more important and higher in rank than its beginning; because it is not observed, and because they deny it while they do not deny the beginning of creation. In the *Kashshaf* it says: It is like your saying: "I have continued to prefer so-and-so and to appoint him as successor over the one I appoint," meaning that the clause "and I appoint him as successor" is neither coordinated with the clause "I prefer", nor included in the predicate of "I have continued"; because you say it before you appoint him, let alone the repeated appointment from you. This is the method of the *Kashshaf*, and it makes the position of "then He repeats it" like the position of an inferential consequence (*tafri'*) upon the interrogative of denunciation.

Know that these two verbs, "yubdi'u" and "yu'idu", and what derives from them, when they have been used together, are like a pair following one another, as in His saying, Most High, ﴿And the falsehood neither originates nor repeats﴾ [Saba': 49] in the chapter of Saba'. In the *Kashshaf* on the chapter of Saba' it says: They made their saying "neither originates nor repeats" a proverb for destruction, and from it is the saying of 'Ubayd:

"Today he neither originates nor repeats"

It is said "abda'a" and "a'ada" in the sense of acting with wide variety, Bishr said:

"My sorrows are a canopy of beginnings and repetitions"

It is also possible that the seeing is cognitive (*'ilmiyyah*), transitive to two objects. He rebukes them for their abandoning of reflection and reasoning that lead to knowledge of how God originates creation then repeats it; because the proofs of the beginning of creation lead the observer to the knowledge that God repeats creation. In this case "thumma" is coordinating the verb "yu'idu" over the verb "yubdi'u", and all of them fall within the scope of denial.

"Kayfa" is an interrogative noun, and it suspends the verb "yarawa" from acting on its object or objects. The meaning: Have they not reflected on this question, that is, on the answer to it? The interrogative with "kayfa" is used for alerting and drawing attention, not for seeking information.

The clause ﴿Indeed, that is easy for God﴾ clarifies what the interrogative implies of denying the non-seeing that leads to knowledge of the occurrence of repetition, since they considered it impossible, whereas if the repetition of creation is not easier than the initial creation in custom, then it is at least equal to it. This is like His saying, Most High: ﴿And He it is who begins creation then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. The reference of "dhalika" (that) is to the verbal noun derived from "yu'idu", like the return of the pronoun to its counterpart in His saying ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum: 27]. The reason for emphasising the sentence with "inna" (indeed) is to refute their claim that it is impossible.

Page 230

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and see how He began creation; then Allah brings about the final creation. Indeed Allah is over all things capable.﴾

This is a transitional interjected clause (i'tiraḍ, a parenthetical insertion) that moves from the rebuke directed at them for neglecting reasoning from what is before their eyes to guiding them to reason from what is far from them: the states of the creation of beings, the succession of nations, and the replacement of some by others. Their habituation to what is before them diverts their minds from contemplating what lies beyond it, namely the signs of its subtleties in what those signs indicate. Therefore God commanded His Messenger to call them to travel through the earth so that they might witness the traces of God's bringing things into being from non-existence, and thus be certain that their re-creation after their passing away is no more wondrous than the initiation of their making.

Travel through the earth was commanded because travel brings the traveller close to many observations from varied lands, with their mountains, rivers and contents, and passes him by the abodes of nations, present and extinct. He sees many things and states he has not become accustomed to seeing. When he witnesses these, the gaze of his reflection roams over their coming into being after non-existence, a roaming that would never have occurred to him when he saw the likes of those creatures in the dwellings of his people. For since he grew up among them from childhood onward, before the faculty of thought arose in his intellect, he became accustomed to passing his sight over them without drawing any inference from their signs. Then, when he witnesses their likes among things that had been absent from his sight, the thought of inference runs through his soul. Travel through the earth is thus a comprehensive means to diverse signs; therefore commanding it for this purpose is among the comprehensive wisdoms.

Regarding the beginning of creation, the past-tense verb was used, because the traveller has no settled place on his path, so he rarely witnesses the occurrence of the beginning of creatures. Rather, he witnesses creatures that were begun earlier, and he realizes that the One who brought them into being did so after they were not, and that He is able to bring about their likes. He is therefore all the more able to re-create them after their non-existence.

Inference from deeds that have already passed is more feasible, because what is settled has a perceptible reality.

In this inference the verb "look" (naẓar) was used, because perceiving what God created is achieved through sight. With the verb of looking, it is more fitting and better known, so that from it one moves to perceiving that He brings about the final creation.

Page 231

Therefore it was followed by the clause ﴿then Allah brings about the final creation﴾, which is an independent clause. "Thumma" ("then") here indicates sequence of rank (al-tartīb al-rutbiyy), as already mentioned in His saying: ﴿then He repeats it﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 19].

The name of Allah is made explicit after its pronoun was previously mentioned in ﴿how He began creation﴾. The apparent expectation would have been "then He brings about". Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "Because the discourse was concerning the restoration, when He established for them that the beginning is from Allah, He argued against them that restoration is a bringing into being like the beginning. So the One whom the beginning did not defeat is the One whom restoration must not defeat. As if He said: then that One who produced the first creation is the One who brings about the final creation. So to alert to this meaning He made His name prominent and placed it as the subject." End of quotation. He means that the shift from the pronoun to the explicit name records the occurrence of this second creation, so that the clause stands independently and serves as a heading of belief, like a proverb. For in the name Allah is the summoning of all the essential attributes by which creation occurs. It also conveys that the subject, reported about by a verbal predicate, carries the meaning of emphasis.

The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things capable﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyīl), meaning: capable of resurrection, and capable of everything when He wills it. The explicit name appears so that the concluding clause stands independently by itself and thus functions like a proverb.

Al-nash'a, on the pattern fa'la, is the single instance of nash', which means bringing into being. This is how the majority of readers recited it. It was expressed in the form of the single instance because it is a sudden creation that differs from the first nash'. It is also said "al-nishā'a", with a long vowel after the shin, on the pattern of al-ka'āba, and similarly al-ra'fa and al-ra'āfa. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "al-nashā'a" with the long vowel. Describing it as "the final" indicates that it is equal to the first creation, so they have no doubt regarding the impossibility of its occurrence. As for His saying: ﴿And you have known the first creation﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 62], that is by way of figurative correspondence in estimation (mushākala taqdīriyya), because His saying before it, ﴿and We will bring you into being in what you do not know﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 61], includes the final creation, so He expressed its content by the term "creation".

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 21:

﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wwills, and to Him you will be turned back.﴾

When he (Allah) mentioned the later creation (al-nash'ah al-akhirah), he followed its mention with the mention of the most important thing it contains and the purpose for which it was brought into existence, which is reward and punishment.

صفحة ٢٣٢
He began with the mention of punishment, because the address is ongoing with those who deny the resurrection, for whom the share is punishment. The two objects of the verbs of willing are omitted, following the common usage with them, and the estimated meaning is: whom He wills to punish and whom He wills to show mercy to. The two groups are known from the verses of promise and threat: the people of promise, Allah wills their mercy, and the people of threat, He wills their punishment. Among those whom He wills to punish are the polytheists, and among those whom He wills to show mercy are the believers. The intended meaning here is both groups together, as indicated by the general address in His words: ﴿and to Him you will be turned back﴾.
Al-qalb (turning) means return, i.e., "and to Him you will be returned."

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing verb is for emphasis and confirmation; the context is not one of restriction (hasr), since there is no rejected belief here. In this is a reaffirmation of the occurrence of the resurrection and an allusion to the threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 22:

﴿And you cannot escape [Allah] on earth or in heaven, and you have no protector or helper other than Allah.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 21], in terms of what it includes of threat (waʿid).

The literal meaning of muʿjiz (one who renders another incapable) is one who makes another unable to do something. Here it is a metaphor for overpowering and escaping from one's control. This was already discussed under His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming, and you cannot escape [it]﴾ [al-Anʿam: 134] in Surat al-Anʿam.

So the meaning is: "And you will not escape the punishment." The object of muʿjizin is omitted because it is known, i.e., "not escaping [Allah]."

The phrase ﴿on earth﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 20] is connected to muʿjizin, meaning: you have no escape on earth, i.e., you will not find a refuge that saves you from Our power over you in any place on earth, whether its plains or its mountains, its deserts or its settled lands.

The conjunction of ﴿or in heaven﴾ with ﴿on earth﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 20] serves as a precaution (iḥtiras) and as a despairing (taʾyis) of hope for salvation, even though they have no hope of ascending to heaven. This is like the saying of al-Aʿsha:

صفحة ٢٣٣

If you were in a pit eighty cubits deep, and were lifted up the ways of the heavens by a ladder.

From the same usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on earth﴾ [Saba': 22]. This addition does not occur in the verse of Surat al-Shura: ﴿And He pardons much, and you cannot escape [Him] on earth; and you have no protector or helper other than Allah﴾ [al-Shura: 30]; because that verse combined address to the believers and the disbelievers with His saying: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is because of what your hands have earned, and He pardons much﴾ [al-Shura: 30], since the pardon is for the believers. The "ma" here is of the accepted hyperbole (mubalagha maqbula), not the imagined kind, as in the saying of Ubayy ibn Sulami al-Dabbi:

Even if a one-hoofed creature had flown before it, it would have flown, but it did not fly.

It is more evident in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass [them]﴾ [al-Rahman: 33]. In this there is an indication of nullifying their deception by the delay of the threat which they had been promised in this world.

When He had despaired them of escaping by their own means in all places, He followed it by despairing them of escaping the threat through the efforts of others, such as allies who intercede to avert punishment from them by means of mediation or intercession, or helpers who defend them by force and power.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 23:

﴿And those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and in His meeting—those have despaired of My mercy, and for those is a painful punishment.﴾

This is an elucidation of His saying: ﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 21]. It is joined (to that verse) because of the additional information it contains, namely that Allah will not bestow mercy upon them, and that a painful punishment will befall them.

The disbelief in the signs of Allah is their disbelief in the Qur'an, and the disbelief in His meeting is the denial of resurrection (al-ba'th).

The demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) indicates that what follows it befell them because of the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative, meaning: they deserved despair from mercy and being struck by the painful punishment because of their disbelief in the Qur'an and their denial of resurrection, in the style of ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5].

Page 234

He reported their despair from the mercy of Allah using the past tense (fi'l al-madi), as a signal of the certainty of its occurrence; the meaning is: "Those will certainly despair of the mercy of Allah."

The use of the explicit noun in His saying ﴿the signs of Allah﴾, rather than a first-person pronoun, serves to honour the signs by attributing them to the Exalted Name, because the Exalted Name carries a reminder that it is worthy that His signs not be disbelieved in. The shift to the first person in His saying "My mercy" is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), by which the style of the speech returns to what the context requires; and the repetition of the demonstrative noun serves to emphasise the warning about their deserving that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 24:

﴿So what was the answer of his people except that they said, "Kill him or burn him." But Allah saved him from the fire. Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾

When the interjected discourse that occurred within the story of Ibrahim was complete, the speech returned to the rest of the story, by mentioning what his people answered him with.

The fa' (فاء, the particle of consequence) is a consequence of the clause ﴿When he said to his people, "Worship Allah"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 16].

The form of restricting the answer (ḥaṣr) was used in His saying ﴿"Kill him or burn him"﴾ to indicate that they did not hesitate in their answer to him, and their word was one in denying him and destroying him, and this is from their firmness in their disbelief.

Then they disagreed about the method of his destruction, between killing by the sword and destroying by burning; then their matter settled on burning him, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But Allah saved him from the fire.﴾ The phrase ﴿jawāba qawmihi﴾ (answer of his people) is the predicate (khabar) of kāna (كان), and its subject (ism) is ﴿an qālū﴾ (that they said). The usual usage is that its subject is placed after it when the "an" is the verbal (maṣdariyyah) "an" with its complement, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The only saying of the believers, when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them, is that they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾ [al-Nur: 51] at the end of Surat al-Nur; and for this reason the noun following the verb kāna in such instances is not read, except in the accusative, in other than the anomalous readings.

Its saving him from the fire has been stated concisely here, and it is explained in detail in Surat al-Anbiya'.

The demonstrative "dhālika" (ذلك, that) refers to the saving from ﴿But Allah saved him from the fire﴾, and that saving was described as "signs" (āyāt) plural and not as one sign; because it is a sign for everyone of his people who witnessed it; and because it indicates the power of Allah, the honour of His Messenger, the fulfilment of His promise, the humiliation of His enemy, and that all creatures, great and small, are subjected to the power of Allah, Exalted is He.

The phrase ﴿a people who believe﴾ (qawmin yu'minūn) was used to indicate that their faith is firmly rooted in them and is among the constituents of their people-hood, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. Thus that is a sign of the great care of Allah, Exalted is He, for His messengers, whereby the people of faith across the various eras affirmed them. In His saying ﴿for a people who believe﴾ there is an implicit allusion that the people of Ibrahim did not affirm these signs, because of the severity of their obstinacy and because faith does not penetrate their minds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 25:

﴿And he said: "You have only taken idols besides Allah as a bond of affection among yourselves in the life of this world; then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disbelieve in others and some of you will curse others, and your refuge is the Fire, and you will have no helpers."﴾

It is possible that this statement of his preceded his being cast into the Fire, and it is possible that it came after Allah had saved him from the Fire. The more apparent reading of the arrangement of the discourse is that it was after Allah had saved him from the Fire. He meant by it to announce their obstinacy against the truth and their persistence in worshipping idols after the proof had become clear to them through the miracle of his being safe from the burning of the Fire. The mention of the idols had preceded shortly before.

The place of restriction with *innama* (إنَّما) is the object of purpose (al-maf'ul li-ajlihi). As for restricting the objects of worship besides Allah to being idols, this was already stated in His words: ﴿Indeed, you worship besides Allah only idols﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 17], meaning: you have taken idols only for the sake of the affection of some of you for others. The basis of the restriction is that no doubt remained for them regarding the worship of idols after witnessing the evidence of the truthfulness of the Messenger who came to nullify them. Thus it becomes certain that the cause of their continuing in the worship of idols is the affection of some of them for others, which impels them to avoid opposing one another. *Al-mawaddah* (the affection) is love and familiarity, and the pronoun in *baynakum* (among you) must necessarily include the idols.

*Al-mawaddah* is love. These people love one another, so none of them opposes the other even if it appears to him that the other is in error; and they love the idols, so they do not abandon their worship even if the evidence of the invalidity of their divinity has become apparent to some of them. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And among the people are those who take besides Allah rivals, loving them as they love Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165].

Al-Fakhr said: That is, affection between the idols and their worshippers. For whoever is overcome by bodily pleasures does not turn to intellectual pleasures, like the insane person when he needs to relieve a need, of eating, drinking, or urinating, while he is among a gathering of notables: he does not heed the intellectual pleasure of modesty and good conduct, but rather he obtains what gives pleasure to his body. Thus they were people of little intellect, so bodily pleasures overcame them, and their intellects did not extend to a non-corporeal object of worship, and they saw those idols adorned with colors and jewels, so they loved them.

The verb *ittakhadtum* (you have taken) is intended to express continuance and persistence in taking them, after the proof of the invalidity of their deserving worship had become clear.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Khalaf read *mawaddatan* in the accusative, with tanwin and without an annexation, and *baynakum* in the accusative as an adverb of place. Hamzah, Hafs from 'Asim, and Rawh from Ya'qub read *mawaddata* in the accusative, without tanwin, rather annexed to *baynikum*, with *baynikum* in the genitive; or it is the annexation of the containing to the container. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Ruways from Ya'qub read it in the nominative and annexed, so that *ma* in *innama* is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and its proper writing is separated; *mawaddah* is the predicate of *inna*. The writing of *innama* as joined is then a non-analogical orthographic convention. The report that it is affection is then a figurative, rational predication, on the basis that taking (the idols) is a consequence of affection. Because there is eloquence in the figurative usage, it carries an emphasis on the predicate after its emphasis by *inna*, so the two emphases take the place of restriction; for restriction is nothing but emphasis upon emphasis, as al-Sakkaki said, meaning that it is equivalent to repeating the predicate, since it affirms and then emphasizes by negating what is other than it.

The statement is used not to convey a judgment but to alert to the error, by the indication of his words following it: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disbelieve in others and some of you will curse others﴾. Similar to it is the relative clause in the verse of 'Abdah ibn al-Tabib:

*Indeed, those you see as your brothers, the cure for the thirst of their hearts is that you be struck down.*

Since in his words "a bond of affection among you" there is an element of establishing a benefit for them in worshipping idols, as through it they acquire mutual affection among themselves that is pleasing to their souls, he joined it with his words: ﴿in the life of this world; then on the Day of Resurrection some of you will disbelieve in others﴾ etc., as an alert to the evil outcome of this affection and a removal of delusion and heedlessness, so that they would know that fleeting pleasures have no value if they bring about lasting regret.

The meaning of ﴿some of you will disbelieve in others﴾ is that those addressed will disbelieve in the idols they used to worship, since on the Day of Resurrection they will deny that they used to worship them.

The meaning of ﴿and some of you will curse others﴾ is that each of those addressed will curse the others, either because the cursed ones deceived the cursers and beautified for them the taking of idols, or because they agreed with them in that.

These are disgraces that befall some of them from others. Then he mentioned what encompasses them of the punishment of humiliation in His words: ﴿and your refuge is the Fire﴾.

Then he mentioned what encompasses them all of the absence of a helper, saying: ﴿and you will have no helpers﴾, thereby negating from them the class of helper, i.e., one who would remove from them that humiliation. The plural was used in negating the helper here, unlike His words earlier: ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 22], because when they conspired against Ibrahim and gathered to support their idols, their recompense was being deprived of supporters, a correspondence between the recompense and the state for which they were requited. Moreover, the singular and the plural within the scope of negation are equal in conveying the negation of every individual of the class.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 26:

﴿So Lot believed in him.﴾

This is a parenthetical sentence placed between the reports about Abraham, in the manner of a consequential insertion (i'tira' al-tafri'). The fa' (so) indicates that Lot hastened to affirm Abraham's truthfulness. Restricting the mention to Lot indicates that no one believed in him except Lot, since he was the single man who believed in him. As for Abraham's wife and Lot's wife, the term "people" (qawm) in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 16], does not include them, because qawm is specific to the men of the tribe. Zuhayr said:

Are they the people of Hisn, or are they women?

In the Torah it is stated that his wife Sarah was with him, and the wife of Lot, whose name was Malikah. Lot was the son of Haran, the brother of Abraham, so Lot at that time was of the community of Abraham, peace be upon them both.

﴿And he said, "Indeed, I am migrating to my Lord; indeed, He is the Almighty, the Wise."﴾

This is coordinated (atf) upon the sentence ﴿So Allah saved him from the fire﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 24].

The pronoun in "he said" refers to Abraham, meaning he declared that he was migrating from the abode of his people, because Allah had commanded him to separate from the people of disbelief.

This was the first migration for the sake of the religion; for this reason He made it a migration "to my Lord." Al-muhajarah is a form of mufa'alah from al-hajr, which is the abandoning of something that one was constantly attached to. The mufa'alah form is for emphasis, or because the one who abandons his people is also abandoned by them.

The particle "ila" (to) in His words ﴿to my Lord﴾ denotes figurative termination (al-intiha' al-majazi), since he made his migration to the land which Allah commanded him to migrate to as though it were a migration to the very essence of Allah, may He be exalted. Thus "ila" serves as an imaginative indicator (takhyil) of a metaphor by allusion (isti'arah makniyyah). Or he made his migration from the place whose people do not worship Allah, seeking a place where there are no associators with Allah, as though it were a migration to Allah; in this case "ila" is used metaphorically for the meaning of the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), a subsidiary metaphor (isti'arah taba'iyyah).

This metaphor is reinforced in both interpretations by His words ﴿indeed, He is the Almighty, the Wise﴾, which is a sentence occupying the position of giving the reason for the content of ﴿Indeed, I am migrating to my Lord﴾; for whoever is mighty, his neighbor and guest take pride in him.

The following of the description "Almighty" with "Wise" serves to convey that His might is firm, placed in its praiseworthy position according to people of intellect, such as supporting the oppressed and supporting the one who calls to the truth. It may also be that "al-Hakim" means "al-Hakim" (the Judge), in which case it is an additional emphasis on the meaning of "al-'Aziz."

The story of Abraham and his people and their lands has already passed in detail in Surat al-Anbiya'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 27:

﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and placed in his offspring prophethood and the Book.﴾
This statement follows the story of Ibrahim (Abraham) to demonstrate his excellence, since it has no connection to the narrative itself. The apparent meaning of "We gave" (wahabna) and "We placed" (ja'alna) is the informing of that fact, so it is part of completing the story, as in Surah Hud. A parallel to this verse has already been mentioned in al-An'am in the context of Ibrahim's virtues. Quran 29:31–32: ﴿When Our messengers came to Abraham with the good news, they said, "We are going to destroy the people of this town. Its people have indeed been wrongdoers." He said, "Indeed, Lot is in it." They said, "We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾

*Lamma* (لَمّا) is a particle that indicates timing. Its basic usage is as an adverb (*zarf*) that must be followed by a clause. What it signifies is the occurrence of one thing upon the occurrence of another: the occurrence of the content of the clause that follows it, at the time the clause it is linked to occurs. It therefore requires two clauses. The first is a past-tense verbal clause, to which *lamma* is attached. The second is a verbal or nominal clause containing something that can be connected to the adverb, such as a verb or a derived noun. The second clause that follows *lamma* is loosely called the "answer of the condition" (*ism al-jaza'*, the conditional response), by way of a figurative usage.

Since *lamma* is an indefinite time adverb, the content of the clause to which it is attached must be known to the listener, because timing means informing the listener of the coincidence of an unknown time with a known time. Thus the presence of *lamma* here implies that the coming of the angels with the good news is a known matter to the listener, even though no mention of the good news has preceded it. Therefore the definiteness of *al-bushra* ("the good news") must be the definiteness of prior reference (*ta'rif al-'ahd*), since *lamma* requires that what it refers to be known. So "the good news" is what was indicated by the words of God, the Exalted, just before: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and placed prophethood and the Book among his descendants﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:27], as its explanation has already passed.

*Al-bushra* is a noun for good news (*bisharah*), which is the report of something that brings joy to the one informed (the *mukhbar*, with the *ba'* vowelled with a fatha). The mention of *bisharah* has already occurred at the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bearer of good news and a warner﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:119], in Surah al-Baqarah.

Among the gentleness of God toward Abraham is that He sent the good news to him before informing him of the destruction of the people of Lot, because He, the Exalted, knew Abraham's forbearance. The meaning is: the angels said to Abraham, "We are going to destroy the people of this town..." and so on.

The "town" (*al-qaryah*) is Sodom (*Sadum*), the town of the people of Lot. Its mention has already passed in Surah al-A'raf.

The clause ﴿Its people have indeed been wrongdoers﴾ is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the destruction. It was intended to comfort Abraham so that he could accept this sorrowful news. It is also because justice requires that punishment should be only for a sin that merits it.

[Page 243]

The wrongdoing is their wronging of themselves through disbelief and indecencies, and their wronging of people by forcing them into indecencies and by accustoming them to them.

His words ﴿Indeed, Lot is in it﴾ are a statement used to remind (Abraham) of God's custom with His messengers, namely the salvation from the punishment that befalls their peoples. This is part of an indirect hint (*ta'rid*) to the angels, by singling out Lot from among those whom the town encompasses in the ruling of destruction. Although Lot was not originally one of the people of the town, his being among them requires concern that the destruction might include him. For this reason he said ﴿Indeed, Lot is in it﴾ using the preposition of location (*fi*), and did not say "from it" (*minha*).

The angels' answer to Abraham, that they know best who is in it, means that they know better than he does the condition of those in the town. This is an answer to what his indirect hint required, namely the reminder of the salvation of Lot. That is: we know better than you the worthiness of Lot for salvation with God, and the worthiness of others for punishment. The angels do not precede God in speech, and they act by His command. Their answer was reassuring to Abraham. Therefore what is meant by their knowledge of who is in the town is their knowledge of the varying conditions of its people, which determine whether they deserve punishment or honour through salvation.

The angels knew this better than Abraham did because their knowledge preceded his, and because it was certain knowledge (*'ilm yaqin*) conveyed by revelation from God concerning what He subjected those angels to. Abraham had not been given any revelation about this matter. Also, their knowledge was detailed, not general, and specific, not universal. For this latter reason they answered with ﴿We know best who is in it﴾, and did not say "We know best about Lot." Their being more knowledgeable than Abraham in this matter does not require that they know more than Abraham in other matters. Abraham possessed the knowledge of prophethood, the sharia, and the governance of the community, whereas the angels glorify God night and day, without slackening, and do not occupy themselves with anything else unless God assigns them to a task. Still less does their being more knowledgeable in this matter require that they be superior to Abraham. The position of the People of Truth is that messengers are superior to angels, and a particular advantage (*mazziyyah*) does not entail overall superiority. Each group has knowledge that God made it aware of and granted it specifically, just as He granted al-Khidr what Moses did not know, and granted Moses what al-Khidr did not know. For this reason God rebuked Moses when he was asked, "Is there anyone more knowledgeable than you?" and he replied, "No." The proper answer would have been to distinguish among the kinds of knowledge.

The clause ﴿We will surely save him and his family﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿We know best who is in it﴾. For this reason it was not joined to it by a conjunction and was separated from it. They knew, by the permission of God, that only Lot and his family would be saved, that is, only his two daughters, and that the rest would perish, including the wife of Lot.

The verb *kanat* ("was") is used in the sense of *takun* ("will be"). It is expressed in the past form to indicate that the event is certain to occur, in the manner of the past event, as in His words ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl 16:1]. It is also possible that what is meant is her being (among those who remain behind) in the knowledge and decree of God, as in the verse of al-Hijr ﴿We decreed that she would be among those who remain behind﴾ [al-Naml 27:57]. In that case the past form is literal.

The discussion of the parallel of His words ﴿except his wife; she is among those who remain behind﴾ has already passed in Surah al-Naml.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 33:

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them, and they said, "Do not fear and do not grieve. Indeed, we will save you and your family, except your wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾

His saying, ﴿Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 31], has indicated that the angels would descend upon the town, and that required that they inform Lot of their arrival at the town, and that they were sent from Allah in response to Lot's request for victory over his people. So this coming was something whose occurrence was decreed, and therefore it was made the condition of the particle lamma (when), as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Ibrahim with the good tidings﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 31].

And "an" (أنْ) is a particle added for emphasis, and it is most often added after "lamma." It serves to confirm the connection between the content of the two clauses that follow "lamma," so it is for confirming the connection between the coming of the messengers and Lot's distress at them. The meaning of confirming it here is the swiftness of the conjunction and the timing between the condition and the consequence, as an alert that the distress followed their coming and struck him without delay. This is because of what is known of the custom of his people in dealing with those who arrived at their town. Lot did not know that they were angels, since they came in the form of men. So the purpose here is to alert that what befell him of distress and constriction of his heart happened before he learned that they were angels who had come to destroy the people of the town, and before they said: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve.﴾

The emphatic "an" did not occur in the verse in Surah Hud, because in that surah there is a detailing of the cause of his distress and constriction of his heart, so that was sufficient in place of alerting to it in this verse. Thus the emphasis here is a kind of ițnab (amplification). The detailed explanation of this was already given in the commentary on Surah Hud.

The verb سِيءَ (was distressed) is built in the passive, because the intended meaning is the occurrence of the effect without regard to its agent.

The clause ﴿and they said, "Do not fear"﴾ is conjoined to it, because it is among what occurred right after the messengers came to Lot. Clauses have been omitted, indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, we will save you﴾, and these are the clauses whose meanings were mentioned in His saying: ﴿And his people came rushing toward him﴾ [Hud: 78] up to His saying: ﴿They said, "O Lot, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you"﴾ [Hud: 81] in Surah Hud. They gave him reassurance before informing him that they were going to bring down punishment upon the people of the town, to hasten his comfort.

The conjoining of "and do not grieve" to "do not fear" combines his reassurance from the harm of the punishment with informing him that those who are about to perish are not worthy of his grief over them, and among them is his wife, because one does not grieve over someone who does not believe in him.

The clause ﴿Indeed, we will save you﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) for the prohibition regarding both matters.

The exception of his wife from the generality of his family is an exception from the causal explanation, not from the prohibition. In this there is an excuse for him regarding the grief that might befall him over the destruction of his wife, although he had considered her sincere toward him. We have explained the reason for this in the commentary on Surah Hud.

This is a resumptive sentence (jumlah musta'nafah) that serves as an explanation of the statement ﴿Fear not and do not grieve﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 33]. It indicates that there is an event one fears and grieves over.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 35:**

﴿And We have certainly left of it a clear sign for a people who use their reason.﴾

It is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause ﴿And [We sent] Lot, when he said to his people﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 28], etc. It is the coordination of one sign with another sign, because the story of Lot is a sign through what it contains of news, and the traces of his people's town are another sign, through what can be observed by those with sight. It is also permissible for it to be a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'taridha*) at the end of the story. In both cases it is part of the speech of God. The "we" (*nun*) of the majestic speaker refers to the Divine Name, and it is not a reference to the angels. The word *al-ayah* (sign) means an indication that points to a matter.

The object of *taraknا* (We left) may be *ayatan* (a sign), so that *min* (from) is a preposition with a genitive object, functioning as a qualifier of *ayatan*, placed before the word it qualifies for emphasis. It is then treated as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of *ayatan*.

It is also permissible for *min* to indicate origin (*ibtida'*), meaning: We left a sign that proceeds from its traces and that makes its news known. It is a clear sign, lasting across a long time up to now. For this reason it is described as *bayyina* (clear). The sign of the ship was not described as *bayyina* in His words ﴿and We made it a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 15], because the ship's planks and iron have decayed, or what remains of it does not appear except after searching, if it remains at all.

It is also permissible to make *min* a noun meaning "some of" (*ba'd*), according to the view of those scholars among the verifiers (*al-muhaqqiqin*) who hold this opinion. In that case *min* is the object, governing a pronoun referring back to *qarya* (town). This has been explained earlier at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God"﴾ [al-Baqara: 8], in the surah of al-Baqara. The meaning is: And We have certainly left from the town traces that indicate to a people who employ their minds in inferring from the traces the conditions of its inhabitants. This sign is the remains of their town, submerged under the water of the Lake of Lot. Through the waters appear the evidences of the town and remnants of the colour of sulphur and the minerals with which their town was stoned. In this there are several proofs, according to the differing faculties of those who reason from them.

The phrase ﴿for a people who use their reason﴾ is connected either to *taraknا* (We left), or it is made a stable adverbial phrase (*zarf mustaqarr*) functioning as a qualifier of *ayatan*.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 36:

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said: "O my people, worship Allah and hope for the Last Day, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief."﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "Lūṭan," which is conjoined to "Nūḥan," the object of "arsalnā" (We sent). So the implied construction is: "And We sent to Madyan their brother Shuʿayb."

The connection in moving from the story of Lot and his people to the story of Madyan and their messenger is that Madyan was among the descendants of Ibrahim (Abraham), and that Allah saved him from the punishment just as He saved Lot.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His words, "ilā Madyan" (to Madyan), serves to achieve conciseness in describing Shu'ayb as their brother, because this description does not apply to Nuh, Ibrahim, or Lut. The meaning of his being a brother to them has already been explained in Surah Hud.

His words, "fa-qāla" (then he said), are a conjunction upon the implied verb, meaning: We sent him, and his sending was followed by his saying.

Al-rajāʾ (hope) means expectation and belief in the occurrence of what is to come. His command to them to await the Last Day indicates that they did not believe in resurrection. The discussion of the parallel of His words, "wa lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍi mufsidīn" (and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief), was given at His words, "kulū wa-ishrabū min rizqi Allāh wa lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍi mufsidīn" (Eat and drink from the provision of Allah, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief) [al-Baqarah: 60] in Surah al-Baqarah.
