Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 37:

﴿So they denied him, and the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes.﴾

Al-akhdh (الأخْذُ): destruction and annihilation. The annihilation is likened to "seizing" (akhdh), on the basis of the common element of removal.

Al-rajfah (الرَّجْفَةُ): a severe quake by which the earth trembles. In Surah Hud it is called al-sayhah (الصَّيْحَةُ, the Cry), because that quake had a violent sound like a shout. The explanation of this has already been given.

In the story of Ibrahim and Lut, reference has been made to what is connected with the purpose for which it is brought here, namely perseverance in conveying the message, patience over the harm of the disbelievers, God's support for them, the punishment of the disbelievers, and the deliverance of the believers.

[p. 248]

﴿And ʿĀd and Thamūd, and it has become clear to you from their dwellings﴾, and Satan made their deeds seem good to them, and he barred them from the way, though they were discerning.

When the mention of the people of Madyan and the people of Lot had passed, the narratives were completed with a reference to ʿĀd and Thamūd, since it is well known in the Qur'an that these nations are mentioned together in the sequence of narratives.

The wāw is conjunctive, joining one narrative to another.

The accusative of ʿĀdan may be governed by a verb that is implied by the context, its estimated form being: "And We destroyed ʿĀd." This is because His saying, exalted is He, just before: ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 37], indicates the meaning of destruction. This was said by al-Zajjāj, and al-Zamakhsharī followed him. It is known that it was a specific destruction by the force of God, exalted is He, so the estimate "And We destroyed ʿĀd" is evident.

It is also permissible for the verb to be estimated as "remember" (udhkur), as is apparent and as is implied in many of the narratives of the Qur'an.

It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with the pronoun in ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 37], the estimate being: "And it seized ʿĀd and Thamūd." It is reported from al-Kisāʾī that it is in the accusative by coordination with ﴿those before them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 3] in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly tested those before them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 3]. But this is remote, because of the great distance between the coordinated element and what it is coordinated with. The more apparent view is that we make it accusative by a verb whose estimate is "And We seized," which is explained by His saying: ﴿So each We seized for his sin﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 40]. This is because kullan (each) is a term that encompasses those mentioned. When it comes in the accusative governed by "We seized," it is determined that what precedes it is in the accusative governed by its like. The nunation of compensation (tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ) attached to kullan is the linking element. The original structure of the sentence is: "And ʿĀd and Thamūd and Qārūn and Pharaoh, etc. . . . each of them, We seized for his sin."

The clause ﴿and it has become clear to you from their dwellings﴾ is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or is a parenthetical clause (muʿtariḍa). The meaning is: it has become clear to you, from seeing their dwellings, that they lived in them, and so they were destroyed to the last one of them.

The dwellings of ʿĀd and Thamūd are well known among the Arabs, and their reports and conditions are transmitted among them, and they pass by them on their journeys to Yemen and to the Levant.

[p. 249]

The implied pronoun in "tabayyana" (it has become clear) refers to the verbal noun derived from the estimated verb, that is: "their destruction or Our seizing of them becomes clear to you."

The clause ﴿and Satan made their deeds seem good to them﴾ is coordinated with the clause "and ʿĀdan and Thamūdan."

Tazyīn (making seem good) means beautifying. The meaning is that he made their shameful deeds seem good to them, and by his whispering he led them to imagine that they were good. This was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We made pleasing to every community their deeds﴾ [al-Anʿām: 108], in Sūrat al-Anʿām.

Ṣadd (barring) is preventing someone from an action, and the "way" (sabīl) here means that which leads to the true objective, which is lasting felicity. Since Satan, by his beautifying of their disbelief, deprived them of the felicity of the Hereafter, it is as if he prevented them from taking a path that would bring them to the beneficial abode.

Istibṣār means being perceptive about matters. The sīn and tā' are for emphasis, like istajāba (he responded), istamsaka (he held fast) and istakbara (he was arrogant). The meaning is that they were people of insight (baṣāʾir), that is, of intellects, so they had no excuse for barring themselves from the way. This clause implies that the error of ʿĀd arose from corruption of belief and from disbelief deeply rooted in them and inherited from their forefathers, and that they were not saved from the punishment of God, because they were able to reflect upon the proofs of God's oneness and the truthfulness of their messengers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 39:

﴿And Qarun, and Pharaoh, and Haman. Certainly Musa (Moses) came to them with clear proofs, but they acted arrogantly in the land, and they were not ones who could escape.﴾

As Allah set forth the example for Quraysh through the nations that denied their messengers, and He took vengeance upon them, in the same way He set forth the example for the chieftains of Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl, Umayya ibn Khalaf, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and Abu Lahab, through the chieftains of some earlier nations. Those chieftains were the cause of the ruin of themselves and the ruin of their people who followed them. This is a warning to Quraysh of what may befall them as a consequence of their leaders' deceiving them and casting them into the danger of a bad end. These three (Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun) were those to whom Musa came with clear proofs. Their stories and the story of Qarun have already been related in Surat al-Qasas.

Page 250

As for what Musa brought to Pharaoh and Haman of clear proofs, these were the miracles with which he challenged them to prove his truthfulness, but Pharaoh turned away from them, and Haman and his people followed him. As for what Musa brought to Qarun, it was his prohibition of insolent exultation (al-bataru).

The words of the Exalted, ﴿but they acted arrogantly in the land﴾, indicate that they disbelieved out of obstinate arrogance and pride, not out of ignorance and folly, as the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah sent him astray knowingly﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23]. Their state was like the state of the chieftains of Quraysh, of whom it cannot be supposed that their intelligence failed to reach the point of certainty that what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought was true and that what the Qur'an brought was truth, but their pride overcame them. The placement of the clause ﴿And Musa certainly came to them﴾ is like the placement of the clause ﴿and it had become clear to you from their dwellings﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 38].

Al-istikbar (arrogance) means intense pride. The sin and the ta' (in istakbaru) are for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿and they were discerning﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 38].

The linking of His saying "fi al-ard" (في الأرض, "in the land") to istakbaru indicates that the arrogance of each of them was throughout all the lands to which he belonged, so this implies that each of these was a lord obeyed in the land.

The definite article in "al-ard" (الأرض, "the land") is for a known reference (al-'ahd). It may be that the known reference is the land of each of them, or that the known reference is the whole terrestrial globe, as an exaggeration of the spread of each one's arrogance throughout the lands, to the extent that it seems to encompass the entire world.

The meaning of "sabq" (escape) in His saying ﴿and they were not ones who could escape﴾ is escaping from the disposal of judgment over them. It has been mentioned in His saying, "And let not those who disbelieved suppose that they have outstripped," in Surat al-Anfal. Here the waw is for the circumstantial state (al-hal), meaning: they acted arrogantly in a state in which their arrogance did not benefit them.

The insertion of the verb "kana" (كان, "was") after the negation is because what is negated is what they supposed to be the result of their arrogance, i.e., that no one could reach them because of their greatness. A similar case is that of Abu Jahl when the two sons of 'Afra' killed him on the day of Badr. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said to him when he found him dying: "Are you Abu Jahl?" He said: "And is there anything greater than a man whom you have killed? If only a farmer had killed me." (i.e., a cultivator, meaning a man of the Ansar, because the Ansar were people of tilling and planting).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 40:

Page 251
﴿So each (of them) We seized for his sin. Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones, and among them were those who were seized by the Cry, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned. And Allah was not to wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾
The fa' (fa) here indicates a consequence (tafri') of the preceding discourse, since it included that Satan made their deeds seem fair to them and (that they were marked by) the arrogance of the others. That is, it was a consequence of that: Allah seized them for their great sins, which arose from Satan's making their deeds seem fair to them and from their arrogance in the land. The thing derived (al-mufarra') is not Allah's seizing them for their sins, because that was already implied by what preceded the derivation. Rather, it was mentioned so that, by mentioning it, one would arrive at a detailed account of the kinds of their seizure, which is His saying: ﴿Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of stones﴾ up to its end. So the fa' in His saying ﴿Among them were those upon whom We sent﴾ ... etc. is for deriving that detail from the generality that preceded it, so that the particularity of the generality followed by the detail is achieved, and to indicate the magnitude of Allah's disposing (of affairs).

As for those upon whom a storm of stones was sent, they are 'Ad. Al-hasib is the violent wind; it was named hasib because it uproots pebbles (hasba') from the earth. Abu Wajza al-Sa'di said:

"I poured upon you my hasib, and left you like the uprooted remnants of 'Ad when the dust covered them."

Here he made the hasib part of what befell 'Ad. The intended people here are not the people of Lot, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a storm of stones, except the family of Lot﴾ [al-Qamar: 34], because the account of the punishment of the people of Lot has just passed in detail, so they do not enter into this generality.
Those seized by the Cry are Thamud, and those whom the earth swallowed are Qarun and his people. The swallowing has already been mentioned in Surat al-Qasas. Those whom He drowned are Pharaoh, Haman, and those with them from their people. This has come in the manner of al-nashr (the enumeration of details) following the order of al-laff (the enfolding summary).

Al-akhdh (seizing) means destruction and annihilation. Annihilation was likened to seizing, by the common feature of removing a thing from its place, so the verb akhadhna was borrowed for it. The wronging of these people is negated of Allah, exalted is He, because their suffering was a recompense for their deeds, and everything that is of the type of recompense is described as justice. Allah has negated the attribute of wronging from Himself, so it is obligatory to believe this by revelation (sam') and not by reason in the station of recompense. As for the station of creation (al-takwin), it is not so.

Page 252
Their wronging themselves is their causing the punishment of their own selves, so they drew punishment upon themselves, because the self is the most deserving of its owner's compassion for it and his reflection on the causes of its good.

The istidrak (qualification) arises from the negation of wronging from Allah regarding their punishment, because it might be imagined from this that the cause of punishment is absent. So the istidrak is to remove this misconception.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 41:

﴿The parable of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider, which takes a house. Indeed, the frailest of houses is the house of the spider, if only they knew.﴾

When the likenesses and parables concerning the nations that took idols besides Allah were made clear to them, and when their idols gave them no benefit once the punishment of Allah came upon them, he followed this with a parable for the condition of all those and for the condition of the polytheists of Quraysh who resembled them in taking what they reckon to be a defence for themselves, though it is too weak to defend even itself. The parable is the spider, which takes for itself a house, thinking that it will shelter itself with it from whoever attacks it. Then, when it is struck by the slightest movement, it does not stand firm or hold, so it collapses and is torn apart. The intended addressees of this speech are the polytheists of Quraysh, and the inclusion of others with them in this is understood through the implied meaning of the discourse (dalalat lahn al-khitab, the indication conveyed by the sense of the speech rather than its explicit wording). The indicator is His saying after it: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows whatever they invoke besides Him, of anything﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 42]. Thus the pronoun in "ittakhadhu" (they took) refers to something known from the context of the speech, namely the polytheists of Quraysh.

The clause "ittakhadhat baytan" (it took a house) is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing the spider, and it is a restriction (qayd) within the comparison (tashbih). This pictured figure, the one used as the comparison, together with the figure being compared, is open to dividing the comparison among its parts. The polytheists resemble the spider in delusion about what they have prepared, and their protectors resemble the spider's house in failing to help those who took them at the time of need, and in vanishing at the least movement. The most benefit they gain from them is a weak benefit, namely dwelling in them and the illusion that they will ward off harm for them, just as polytheists take comfort in their delusions about their idols. This is a remarkable parable (tamthil), one of the novel formulations of the Qur'an, as will come shortly in His saying: ﴿And these parables We strike for people, in this surah﴾.

The "'ankabut" (spider) is a kind of insect with a belly and legs. There are three kinds of it. Among them is a kind called "laith al-'anakib" (the lion of spiders), which preys on flies. All of them make for themselves a web which they weave from their saliva, consisting of threads stretched between two ends of a tree or walls. In the middle of those threads they make a thicker side, with more connected threads, in which they hide and lay their eggs. It is called a "bayt" (house) because of its resemblance to a tent, in that it is woven and fastened at its edges, so it is like a Bedouin tent (bayt al-sh'ir).

The clause ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾ is an interposed clause (mu'taridah) that makes clear the aspect of resemblance. This clause functions as a proverb (mathal), used for the scarcity of benefit from something. This requires that the religions whose adherents worship other than Allah are the most contemptible of religions and the furthest from goodness and right guidance, even though they vary in the errors that afflict those forms of worship, just as spider webs vary in thickness according to the variation in the strength and weakness of the small creatures that weave them.

The clause ﴿if only they knew﴾ is connected to the clause ﴿like the spider﴾, not to the clause ﴿And indeed the frailest of houses is the house of the spider﴾. So the answer to "law" (if) is to be understood as follows: "If only they knew" that this is their parable, that is, but they do not know that what they took brings no help to them. As for the frailty of the spider's house, no one is ignorant of it.

[Page 253]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 42:

﴿Indeed, Allah knows what they call upon besides Him of anything. And He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ "

When He negated from them knowledge of what the parable contained of the baseness of their idols, which they worship, and the scarcity of their benefit, by His saying: ﴿If only they knew﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 41], which implies that they do not know, He followed it by informing them of His knowledge of the minute details of the states of those idols, despite their differences and the differences in the beliefs of the tribes that worshipped them. And among the effects of His knowledge of them is His coining that parable for the state of those who worship them and for their own state as well. This is a means of pushing them to suspect their own intellects, and that it is incumbent upon them to reflect on the realities of things, as an implicit rebuke of the deficiency of their knowledge, like His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah knows and you do not know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216]. This is therefore a reproach to them for their negligence regarding knowledge of the realities of matters, which Allah knows, and whose rational proofs and historical parallels He has made clear to them, and which He brought close to them through sensory illustrations. Yet they were blind and deaf to this and that.

The "mā" in His saying ﴿what they call upon﴾ may be negative, suspending the verb "yaʿlamu" (knows) from acting, and "min" (of) is then a superfluous particle for emphasis of the negation, and its object is in meaning the object of "tadʿūna" (you call upon), the movement of the superfluous preposition appearing on it. The meaning of the speech is: Allah knows that you call upon no existent thing, but rather you call upon non-existent matters. In this there is a belittling of their idols by making them like non-existence, because they are empty of all the attributes fitting to divinity. So they are, in their category, like non-existence. Since they resemble non-existent things in the absence of the claimed benefit, the construction denoting negation of existence is used for them by way of the figurative mode. The hearer does not suppose that the intent is to deny that they called upon friends besides Allah, because the context, both preceding and following, rejects this. This is like His saying the Exalted: ﴿The Christians are not upon anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113] in Surat al-Baqarah, and ﴿You are not upon anything﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 68] in Surat al-Ma'idah, and like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when he was asked about soothsayers: "They are not anything" (ﷺ), meaning they are not anything in what they claim of knowledge of the unseen.

The essential meaning: from His knowledge, exalted is He, that they are existents like non-existence, He coined for them a parable with the spider's house, and for their worshippers a parable with the spider that took it. On this view the speech is explicit in invalidating the divinity of the idols and in that they are like non-existence.

It is also permissible that "mā" be interrogative, suspending the verb "yaʿlamu" from action, in the manner of their saying: "I know whether Zayd is standing," meaning: I know its answer. And "min" is explanatory of the indefiniteness in the interrogative "mā," meaning: some thing among the many called-upon beings among the nations. In this there is an implicit rebuke that the polytheists do not know the answer to the questioner's question "What do you call upon besides Allah?" That is, Allah has known that, and from His knowledge of that is that He coined for them the parable of the spider that took a house, and for the worshipped beings a parable of the spider's house. Were you asked, "What do you call upon besides Allah?", you would stammer and not produce an answer, for the nature of false beliefs and sick understandings is that their holder cannot state them verbally or explain them, since, being composed of incompatible assertions, their holder cannot establish them, and he does not remain long before his corrupt belief is exposed, through his inability to articulate it.

Some exegetes made "yaʿlamu" here transitive to one object and meaning "yaʿrifu" (recognises), and made "mā" a relative pronoun, the object of "tadʿūna," with the returning pronoun omitted. This is objected to because attributing knowledge in the sense of recognition, which is transitive to one object, to Allah amounts to attributing the act of recognition to Allah, on the basis of distinguishing between the verb "ʿalima" and the verb "ʿarafa" according to those who define recognition as perceiving a thing through its traces and sensible properties, and who hold that it is weaker than knowledge, because knowledge is common for knowing the realities and relations of things.

From al-Khalil ibn Ahmad: "Knowledge consists of two kinds of cognition that are combined. In your saying ʿaraftu Zaydan qa'iman (I recognised Zayd standing), 'standing' is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of 'Zayd'; and in your saying ʿalimtu Zaydan qa'iman (I knew Zayd standing), 'standing' is a second object of 'ʿalimtu'." End of quotation. He means that the verb "ʿarafa" denotes one perception, which is perception of the essence, while the verb "ʿalima" denotes two perceptions: perception of the essence and perception of the establishment of a judgement concerning it, in the manner that the logicians have stated regarding conception and assent. Therefore the act of recognition has not been attributed to Allah in the Book or the Sunnah, so how could what amounts to its meaning be attributed to Him?

The clause ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah knows﴾, because the clause, on both meanings of "mā," indicates that He who made clear the baseness of the state of the idols and the disorder of the minds of their worshippers did not heed exposing and unveiling them in a manner that would distress them, despite the abundance of their followers and the illusions that no one harms them without them being an aid against him. So if the idols had any share in divinity, whoever belittles them would not escape their harm, as in His saying: ﴿Say: If there were with Him other gods, as you say, they would surely have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ [al-Isra': 42], as previously mentioned. And since He exposed the minds of their worshippers, He did not fear them on behalf of His friends, let alone for His own Self. He is the Mighty who is not overcome, and the Wise whom illusions and sophistries do not deceive, unlike the state of those and those.

The majority read "tadʿūna" with the second person (fawqiyyah), in the manner of the iltifat (shift of grammatical person), and Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ya'qub read it with the third person (taḥtiyyah).

After Allah had explained to them the corruption of their belief in idols, and followed that with a reproach for their ignorance of it, He here censures them for not being fit to grasp those proofs that were brought near to them through the method of parable (*tamthil*, illustrative comparison). The demonstrative pronoun is clarified by the substituted noun that follows it, which is "the parables" (*al-amthal*).

[Page 256]

The demonstrative refers to something present in minds, for everyone who heard the Qur'an had some of these parables fixed in his mind. The demonstrative is used to draw attention to the parables struck in the Qur'an, among which is this parable of the spider.

The clause ﴿We strike them for the people﴾ is a predicate of the demonstrative. This informative clause is used to express favour and kindness, because striking parables brings the subtle matters closer to understanding. Al-Zamakhshari said: The Arabs' striking of parables, and the scholars' citing of examples and analogues, is a matter that is not obscure in bringing out hidden meanings and lifting the veils from realities, so that he shows you the imagined in the form of the established, and the absent as if it were witnessed. The excellence of striking parables has already been explained at the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito or what is above it﴾ (al-Baqarah: 26), in Surat al-Baqarah.

For this reason, this clause is followed by the clause ﴿and none will understand them except those of knowledge﴾. Here "reason" (*al-'aql*) means understanding, i.e., none comprehends their purpose except those whose intellects are complete, so that they are scholars and not foolish of mind. In this there is an implicit rebuke that those who did not benefit from them are deficient in intellect. How much more so, then, are those who turned away from reflecting on their indication and took them as a mockery and derision. When the Quraysh heard His saying, ﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it. And if the fly should steal from them a thing, they could not recover it from it﴾ (al-Hajj: 73), and His saying, ﴿Like the spider that takes a home﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 41), they said: Muhammad is not ashamed to give as examples the fly, the spider, and the mosquito. This is from their slander; for the eloquent know that every situation has its appropriate speech, and every word has its own proper context.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 44:

﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth. Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾

After Allah, exalted is He, had made clear that the polytheists did not benefit from the proof, its premises and its conclusions, which lead to the invalidity of the divinity of the idols, the proof having been fully set out, sufficient for whoever wishes to contemplate and reflect upon the soundness of its premises with fairness, the discourse turned to addressing the believers, to draw attention to the standing of the believers, since they benefited from something more subtle than that, namely the state of looking and reflecting upon the indications of created beings that their Creator is Allah, and that nothing other than Him is worthy of sharing in His divinity. Thus it conveys that the believers have come to know, through guidance, the invalidity of the divinity of the idols, unlike the polytheists who were not guided by this. From this it is understood that those who do not reflect upon them are not people of knowledge, taking this from the implication of the attribute in His saying "for the believers," if the descriptive meaning of "for the believers" is considered; or taking it from the restriction to mentioning the believers in His saying ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers﴾, if the designation "the believers" is considered a title.

The restriction, when mentioning the evidence of the Oneness of God, to the benefit of the believers from that indication, which implies that the polytheists did not benefit from it, resembles the ihtibak (interlacing) between the two verses.

The ba' in "bil-haqq" (with truth) denotes accompaniment (mulaabasah), i.e., He created them in all their conditions with that which is not vain. Vanity (batil) in anything is that which does not fulfill what it was made for. The opposite of vanity is truth (haqq), so truth in every work is its perfection and the attainment of the purpose intended from it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27].

What is meant by "the heavens and the earth" is what includes their essence and the existents contained within them. This perfectly crafted creation, in which there is no shortfall from what was intended from it, is a sign of the Oneness of the Creator and of the attributes of His essence and His acts.

[Page 258]

After God set forth for people the parables of the earlier nations, He brought the clear proof that refutes the beliefs of the polytheists. He affirmed the soundness of the beliefs of the believers with the highest degree of clarity, beyond which nothing more is needed. Then He addressed His Messenger with an address that strengthens his resolve to spread the call, to persist in the sacred laws, and to proclaim the word of God in this way. It also contains what increases the righteousness of the believers, who have benefited from the proofs of God's oneness. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is an exemplar for the believers and their leader, so his command is a command to them too, as indicated by the concluding statement, "And God knows what you do," which uses the plural form of address, like His saying: ﴿So go straight as you have been commanded, and [so too] those who turned with you [to God]﴾ [Hud: 112]. He commanded him to recite the Qur'an, since he had neglected nothing of its guidance.

[Page 258 continues]

The object of the verb "recite" (utlu) is omitted so that the recitation applies to both Muslims and polytheists. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred... and to recite the Qur'an. Whoever is guided is guided only for his own soul, and whoever goes astray, say: I am only one of the warners﴾ [al-Naml: 91–92].

He commanded him to establish the prayer because prayer is a great act of worship. This command includes the community, for the command to establish prayer is repeated in many verses.

He justified the command to establish prayer by pointing to the psychological benefit it contains, saying: "Indeed, prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing." The particle "inna" here functions like the causal "fa" (for), i.e., it introduces a reason. There is no doubt that this justification is addressed to the community, since the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is protected from indecency and wrongdoing. So the reason is given for the command to establish prayer, but not for the command to recite the Qur'an, because of the divine secret placed in prayer, which people cannot discover except by guidance from God, exalted is He. He informed them that prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing; the meaning is that it forbids the one who prays.

Since the literal sense of forbidding does not apply to prayer itself, the verb "tanha" (forbids) must be understood in a figurative sense (majaz, a non-literal usage based on a relation or resemblance). The intended meaning is that prayer facilitates for the one who prays the abandonment of indecency and wrongdoing. It does not mean that prayer necessarily prevents the worshipper from committing indecency and wrongdoing, for experience contradicts this: how many a worshipper establishes his prayer yet commits some indecency and wrongdoing?

Nor is it correct to take it to mean that prayer turns the worshipper away from indecency and wrongdoing for as long as he is engaged in performing it, since this meaning is of little benefit. Most actions keep the one engaged in them from engaging in other things.

Since the verse is directed toward praising prayer and explaining its excellence in religion, the intended meaning must be that prayer warns against indecency and wrongdoing with a warning that is among its distinctive features.

The commentators have various ways of explaining this. Among them is what some have said: that what is meant is the reward prayer has with God, for that is a different purpose and not directly aimed at abandoning indecency and wrongdoing, but it is one of the means of multiplying good deeds so that they may outweigh bad deeds. Thus, to explain this verse in an acceptable way, we must take its ruling as general for every prayer, not limited to the prayers of the righteous. By this, several interpretations that they gave to the verse fall away.

[Page 259]

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "In my view, that is because the one who prays, if he observes what is obligatory of humility and submission, his soul is purified by it, and the awareness of God's watchfulness settles within it, so this continues in his words and deeds, and he refrains from indecency and wrongdoing." End of quote. But this involves conditions in prayer that do not fit a general statement, although they are among the features of prayer that Muslims should be taught when they first learn the foundations of Islam.

My view on the meaning of the verse is that the verb "tanha" (forbids) should be understood as the closest figurative sense to the literal: namely, likening what prayer comprises to a forbidding, and likening prayer, in comprising it, to one who forbids. The point of resemblance is that prayer contains reminders of God, through words and actions, which for the worshipper are like a preacher who reminds him of God, exalted is He, since the preacher forbids his listener from committing what does not please God. This is like the saying: "Your friend is a mirror in which you see your faults." In prayer there are words: magnifying God (takbir), praising Him (tahmid), glorifying Him (tasbih), turning to Him in supplication and seeking forgiveness, reciting the Opening chapter, which contains praise and glorification of God, acknowledging servitude to Him, asking Him for help and guidance, and avoiding what angers Him and what is misguidance. All of these remind one to seek God's pleasure and to desist from disobedience to Him and from what leads to His wrath. This is a barrier against indecency and wrongdoing.

In prayer there are actions that express submission and humility to God, such as standing, bowing, and prostrating. This reminds one of the necessity of seeking His pleasure and staying far from His anger. All of this is among the things that turn one away from indecency and wrongdoing.

In prayer there are also inner acts: intention, and preparation to stand before God. This reminds one that the One worshipped deserves that His commands be obeyed and His prohibitions avoided.

Thus prayer, taken as a whole, is like a preacher forbidding indecency and wrongdoing. God said "forbids" (tanha) and did not say "turns away," "prevents," or anything similar that would imply diverting the worshipper from indecency and wrongdoing.

[Page 260]

Then people differ in their abstention, and this sense of prohibition against indecency and wrongdoing is among the wisdoms behind making the prayers distributed over times of the day and the night, so that the reminder is renewed and the admonitions follow one another. In proportion to the repetition of this, the thoughts of piety increase in souls, and the soul distances itself from disobedience until piety becomes a settled disposition (malaka) for it. Beyond this there is a divine property which God placed in prayer, by which the abstention from indecency and wrongdoing is facilitated.

Ahmad, Ibn Hibban and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Hurayra who said: "A man came to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and said: 'So-and-so prays at night, but when morning comes he steals.' He said: 'His prayer at night will forbid him from what you say.'"

Know that the definite article in His saying, "indecency and wrongdoing" (al-fahsha' wa al-munkar), is the definite article of genus. So whenever the worshipper, during his prayer, remembers the greatness of his Lord and the obligation to obey Him, and recalls what he may do of indecency and wrongdoing, his prayer at that moment has forbidden him from some instances of indecency and wrongdoing.

Al-fahsha' is the noun for fahisha (indecency), and fuhsh is going beyond the acceptable limit. So what is meant by fahisha is an act that exceeds what is acceptable among people. What was mentioned before in His saying, "He only commands you to evil and indecency," in Surat al-Baqara, applies. What is intended here by fahisha is going beyond the limit that is permitted by the law in speech and action, and by munkar is what one disapproves of and does not accept its occurrence.

It seems that the joining of indecency and wrongdoing is viewed in terms of the different aspect of their blameworthiness and the prohibition against them.

His saying, "And the remembrance of God is greater," may be a conjunction with the clause, "Indeed, prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing," so that it is a conjunction of one reason with another reason. The remembrance of God here means prayer, as in His saying: ﴿Hasten to the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Jumu'a: 9], meaning the Friday prayer. The shift from the word "prayer," which functions almost as a proper name for it, to expressing it through an idafa (genitive construction) indicates the reason why prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing: that is, it forbids them because it is the remembrance of God, and the remembrance of God is a great matter. So the elative form (ism al-tafdil) here has lost its comparative sense and is intended to express the strength of the attribute, as when we say "God is greatest" (Allahu akbar), and do not mean that He is greater than some other great thing.

[Page 261]

It may also be a conjunction with the clause, "Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book." The meaning would then be: "Remember God, for the remembrance of God is a great matter." So the remembrance here may mean recollecting the greatness of God, exalted is He. It may also mean the remembrance of God by the tongue, so as to include the remembrance of God during prayer and outside it. The elative form here too has lost its comparative sense, and it is in the sense of the saying of Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "No human being has done a deed that saves him from the punishment of God more than the remembrance of God."

It may also mean by remembrance the recollection of what God commanded and prohibited, that is, watchfulness over God, exalted is He, and fear of His anger. In that case the elative keeps its comparative sense: "And the remembrance of God is greater [in forbidding indecency and wrongdoing] than the prayer in that forbidding," because this remembrance can be repeated more often than prayer is repeated. This is close to the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "The best of the thanks to God by the tongue is the remembrance of God at His command and His prohibition."

You may also say: the remembrance of God is faith in His existence and that He is one. When He commanded His Messenger and intended to command the believers with two great acts of righteousness, He followed this with the statement that faith in God is greater than these, since it is the root, as in His saying: ﴿Freeing a neck﴾ [al-Balad: 13], ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ [al-Balad: 14], ﴿an orphan near of kin﴾ [al-Balad: 15], ﴿or a needy man in misery﴾ [al-Balad: 16], ﴿then being among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17]. This is a case of the back (ajuz) returning to the front (sadr), and by it the discourse returns to magnifying the matter of monotheism and denouncing polytheism, from His saying: "Indeed God knows whatever they call upon besides Him, of anything" [al-'Ankabut: 42], up to this point.

His saying, "And God knows what you do," is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes it. It is both a promise and a warning, in view of what His saying "Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book and establish the prayer" contains, and His saying "forbids indecency and wrongdoing."

Al-sun' means action.

[Page 5]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Surah al-'Ankabut

﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in the best manner, except for those of them who have wronged. And say: "We believe in what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to you. Our God and your God is one, and we are Muslims to Him."﴾

This is a conjunction with the clause ﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45], and so on, in view of what that entails of abandoning the polytheists and refraining from disputing with them, following His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And these are the parables We present to the people, but none understands them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43], as has already been mentioned just above. This was a preparation for what would occur of the call in Medina after the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration, because disputing with the People of the Book would not arise for the Prophet (ﷺ) or the believers in Mecca. But since the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was at the time of the revelation of the final verses of this surah on the verge of migrating to Medina, and the preceding verses were a harsh disputation against the polytheists through the depiction of their state by the state of the spider, and His saying: ﴿but none understands them except the knowledgeable﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43], God prepared for His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, the method of disputing with the People of the Book. Thus this verse is an interjection between the argument with the polytheists and the return to it in His saying: ﴿And so We have revealed to you the Book﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 47] and the verses that follow.

The prohibition is phrased in the plural so that it includes the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, since the Muslims may encounter disputations with the People of the Book in the absence of the Prophet (ﷺ) or before his arrival in Medina.

Al-mujadalah (disputation) is a form of the verb from al-jadal, which is establishing proof for an opinion about which its holder differs with another. It has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿And do not dispute on behalf of those who betray themselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 107] in Surah al-Nisa'. From this it is known that this verse has no connection with the ruling on fighting the People of the Book, such that one would move from that to whether it was abrogated (naskh, i.e., replacement of a ruling by a later one) or whether its ruling remains; for that would take it out of its proper course.

Disputation occurs both in times of peace and in times of fighting.

The People of the Book, in the terminology of the Qur'an, are the Jews and the Christians, and what is intended here is the Jews, for they were the ones who were numerous in Medina and the villages around it. It also includes the Christians if a disputation with them arises, like what arose with the Christians of Najran.

﴿The best manner﴾ [al-Isra': 53] is an exception from an omitted element indicated by the exception stated. Its estimated meaning is: "Do not dispute with them with any dispute except with that which is the best manner."

"Ahsan" (best) is an elative form (ism al-tafdil) which may be on its basic meaning, so that the element of comparison is supplied from what the context indicates, i.e., "in a better manner than your disputation with the polytheists," or "in a better manner than their disputation with you," as the form of the verbal noun indicates.

It may also be that the elative form is stripped of comparison for the sake of intensifying the goodness, i.e., "except with the goodly disputation," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125] at the end of Surah al-Nahl. God gave the Prophet (ﷺ) the choice in disputing with the polytheists between arguing with them in goodness, as the verse of Surah al-Nahl requires, and arguing with them with severity, like His saying: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites and be harsh with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73]. For harshness encompasses all dealings, and among them disputations, and is not restricted to the specific matter of jihad, since jihad in its entirety is harshness. Therefore the conjunction of harshness with jihad would be nothing but a harshness other than jihad.

The reason for the injunction to goodness in disputing with the People of the Book is that the People of the Book believe in God and do not associate partners with Him. Thus they are qualified to accept proof, and they are not presumed to be obstinate. Also, the etiquette of their religion and their Book has given them knowledge of the method of disputation. Therefore it is fitting that in disputing with them one restricts oneself to explaining the proof without harshness, out of caution against repelling them. By contrast, the polytheists have shown such rigidity, arrogance, and coarseness that one is discouraged from persuading them by theoretical proof. It has been specified that they are to be treated with severity and that their religion be vilified and their way be denounced at length, because that is closer to affecting them.

Thus this should be the condition at the beginning of disputing with the People of the Book, and to the extent that the hope of their being guided allows, by way of gentleness. If they meet goodness with its opposite, the ruling shifts to the exception in His saying: ﴿except for those of them who have wronged﴾.

Those of them who have wronged are those who were obstinate and openly displayed enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims, and refused to accept the call. These wronged the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims out of envy and hatred, because Islam had come to abrogate their law (naskh), and they began scheming against the Prophet (ﷺ), and the hypocrites arose from among them. All of this is injustice and aggression.

The Jews had been at peace with Islam before the migration of the Muslims to Medina, and they used to say that Muhammad was "the messenger of the unlettered," as Ibn Sayyad said when the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Do you testify that I am the Messenger of God?" He said: "I testify that you are the messenger of the unlettered." Then when he came to Medina, he called them on the first day he arrived, which was the day 'Abd Allah ibn Salam embraced Islam, and from that day they began to disown Islam.

The conjunction of ﴿And say: "We believe"﴾ to the end of the verse is an instruction for the introduction to disputation in the best manner. This is among what is called clarifying the point of contention and narrowing the gap of disagreement. It is the establishment of the methods of obligation (ilzam) in debate, which is to say: "We have agreed on such and such, so let us argue about what lies beyond that." What they are commanded to say here is among what both parties agree upon, so it should be the path to concord, and it is not included in the sphere of disputation, because disputation occurs at the point of difference. Moreover, what they are commanded to say here is a report of what the Muslims believe, whereas disputation occurs regarding what the People of the Book believe that contradicts the beliefs of the Muslims, like His saying: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 65] down to His saying: ﴿nor was he of the polytheists﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67].

Because the content of this verse does not fall within the sphere of disputation, it is conjoined to what precedes it. Had it been among what disputation encompasses, that would require separating it, since it is like badal al-ishtimal (a comprehensive apposition).

The meaning of ﴿what has been revealed to us﴾ is the Qur'an.

Expressing it by this relative clause alerts to the error of the People of the Book, since they denied that God would send down a Book to other than their prophets. For this reason He followed it with: ﴿and what has been revealed to you﴾. His saying: ﴿and what has been revealed to you﴾ is a conjunction of the relative clause of an omitted relative noun, which is indicated by what precedes it. The estimated meaning is: "and that which has been revealed to you," i.e., the Book, which is the Torah, by the indication of His saying "to you." The meaning is: "We believe in your Book, so you should not turn away from us." This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, do you resent us only because we believe in God and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 59]. Likewise His saying: ﴿Our God and your God is one﴾ is a reminder that the believers and the Jews believe in one God. These are two foundations on which many of the adherents of religions differ.

His saying: ﴿and we are Muslims to Him﴾ is intended for both parties: the party of the speakers and the party of the addressees. It thus encompasses the Muslims and the People of the Book. Accordingly, the sense of "Muslims" here is one of its two usages, namely submitting one's face to God, i.e., not associating anything with Him. That is: "And both of us are Muslims to God, exalted is He, we do not associate anything else with Him." The fronting of the prepositional phrase ﴿to Him﴾ before its governing verb in ﴿Muslims to Him﴾ is for the purpose of restriction (ikhtisas), an indirect reproach to the polytheists who did not single out God for divinity.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 47:

﴿And thus have We sent down to you the Book. Those to whom We have given the Book believe in it, and among these there are those who believe in it. And none deny Our signs except the disbelievers.﴾

This is a return to the argument against the polytheists concerning the proof that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah to His Messenger ﷺ.

The meaning is: and like this wondrous revelation, We have sent down to you the Book, which is wondrous in its eloquence, the nobility of its meanings, the sweetness of its structures, and its superiority over every speech of the eloquent, and in its being revealed in stages (tanjim), and other than that. The explanation of this kind of indication has already passed at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And thus We have made you a median community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah.

From the wondrousness of its revelation follows the report that those whom Allah has taught the Book believe in it, that is, they affirm that it is from Allah; because they are more knowledgeable of the styles of the books revealed to the messengers and prophets, and more aware of the marks and characteristics of the messengers.

He said ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ rather than saying "the People of the Book" (ahl al-Kitab), because in ﴿We have given them the Book﴾ there is a reminder to them that they are trustees of it, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿by what they were entrusted to preserve of the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44].

The present tense (fi'l mudari') is used either to indicate that it will occur in the future, or to indicate the continual renewal of the belief of this group in it, that is, the belief of those among them who believe is ongoing, and the number of believers increases day by day.

The indication by ﴿these﴾ (ha'ula') refers to the people of Makkah, treating them as those present at the time of the revelation of the verse, because they are present in the mind through the frequent observation of their conditions and their disputes. Such is the usage of the Qur'an, where it mentions "these" without prior mention of anything suitable to refer to, and Allah has inspired me with this; it was already mentioned at His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If these disbelieve in it﴾ [al-An'am: 89] in Surat al-An'am. The meaning: among the polytheists of Makkah there are those who believe in it, that is, that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah; and these are those who embraced Islam and those who will embrace it later. Among them are some who believe in it inwardly but do not manifest that, out of obstinacy and arrogance, like al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And none deny Our signs except the disbelievers﴾ indicates that among these who believe in the Qur'an, from the People of the Book and the people of Makkah, there are those who conceal their faith, denying it out of their firmness in disbelief.

The definite article in ﴿al-kafiruna (the disbelievers)﴾ indicates the meaning of completeness in the described attribute, that is: none except those who are deeply immersed in disbelief and firmly rooted in it, so that the difference between "yajhadu (deny)" and "al-kafirun" becomes apparent; for without the indication of the meaning of completeness the sense of the speech would become: "and none deny except the deniers."

He referred to the Book as "signs" (ayat) because it consists of signs indicating that it is from Allah, by reason of its inimitability (i'jaz), its challenge (tahaddi), and the inability of the obstinate to produce a surah like it.

This is primarily directed at the polytheists, because their denial has actually occurred; and in it is a preparation for its application to whoever among the People of the Book may deny it, without confronting them directly by calling them disbelievers, since he has not known that of them yet; but if they do so, they have brought that upon themselves.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 48:

Page 10
﴿You did not recite any Scripture before it, nor did you write one with your right hand; for then the falsifiers would have had doubts.﴾
This is an argument from the attribute of being unlettered (ummiyyah), which the Messenger ﷺ was known for, and its indication that he was revealed to by God is the greatest of indications. This argument appears in the Qur'an in several places, such as His saying: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [al-Shura: 52], and His saying: ﴿Indeed I have dwelt among you a lifetime before it. Will you not reason?﴾ [Yunus: 16].

The meaning of ﴿You did not recite any Scripture before it﴾ is that you were not reading any book until someone might say: this Qur'an that he brought is what he used to recite before.

﴿Nor did you write it﴾ means: you did not write a book even if you did not recite it. The purpose is the negation of both states of learning, namely learning by reading and learning by writing, thoroughly establishing the attribute of being unlettered. For one who memorizes a book without knowing how to write is not counted as unlettered, like the blind scholars, and one who can write what is dictated to him without memorizing knowledge is not counted as unlettered, like the copyists. Thus, with the negation of both recitation and writing, the attribute of being unlettered is established.

"Idhan" (then, in that case) is an answer and a response to a hypothetical condition introduced by "law" (if); because it is a supposition indicated by His saying: ﴿You did not recite﴾ and ﴿nor did you write it﴾. The estimate is: if you had recited a Scripture before it or written it, the falsifiers would have had doubts. The occurrence of the answer of "idhan" accompanied by the lam, with which the answer of "law" commonly appears, is an indication that the implied condition is a conditional with "law", as in the verse of Qurayt al-'Anbari:

If I were of Mazin, the sons of Laqit of Dhuhl, the son of Shayban, would not have plundered my camels,
then there would have risen to my defense a rough folk, when the protector is in a fit of rage, were one with madness to be soft.

Al-Marzuqi said in his "Sharh al-Hamasa": "The benefit of 'idhan' is that he put the second line in the manner of an answer to one who said to him: and if they had plundered your camels, what would the sons of Mazin have done? So he said:

Then there would have risen to my defense a rough folk."
It is also permissible that "then there would have risen" is the answer to "law", as if it was answered with two answers. This is like when you say: If you were free, you would have found disgusting what slaves do; then you would have found admirable what free people do. End quote. That is, it is permissible that the clause "then there would have risen" is a substitute for the clause "would not have plundered".

The discussion of its parallel has already preceded in His saying: ﴿God has not taken any son, and there was not with Him any god; otherwise each god would have gone off with what he created﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91], in Surat al-Mu'minun. "Irtiyab" (doubt): the occurrence of suspicion in the soul, which is doubt.

The connection between the recitation and writing, which preceded the revelation of the Qur'an, and the occurrence of doubt in the souls of the polytheists is that if that had been happening, it would have been possible in their view that the Qur'an was of the kind of what he used to recite before from earlier books, and that it was something he had written before from speech he had received, and then rose today to spread it and call with it.

He made that a cause of doubt rather than a cause of certain denial, because the composition of the Qur'an, its eloquence, and what it contains of meanings nullify that it is of the type of what preceded of books, narratives, sermons and poetry. But since that requires reflection, it did not prevent the passing of a thought of doubt in general before completing consideration and reflection, such that persistent doubt would be slander and obstinacy.

The qualification of ﴿write it﴾ with the phrase "with your right hand" is for emphasis, since writing is only done with the right hand; it is like His saying: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38].

Describing the deniers as "falsifiers" (mubtilun) is considered in regard to their actual state; for they denied while the suspicion of falsehood was absent, so their denial now was false, and they are falsifiers who go deep into falsehood. Thus the discussion of describing them as falsifiers is like the discussion of describing them as disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 49:

﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge. And none deny Our signs except the wrongdoers.﴾

"Rather" (bal) is a retraction of what the hypothesis in His words ﴿Otherwise, the falsifiers would have had doubt﴾ implies. That is: rather, the Qur'an is such that no doubt can reach it that it is from Allah. All of it is signs indicating the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ and that it is from Allah, because of the inimitability (i'jaz) it contains in its wording and meaning, and because of the circumstance that supports this inimitability: the one who brought it was unlettered (ummi), who did not recite any book before it nor write. That is: rather, the Qur'an consists of signs that were not among the things recited before its revelation; rather, it is signs in the breast of the Prophet ﷺ.

So what is meant by the breasts of those who have been given knowledge is the breast of the Prophet ﷺ, expressed in the plural as an act of honouring him.

The knowledge that was given to the Prophet ﷺ is prophethood, as in His saying, ﴿And We gave David and Solomon knowledge﴾ [al-Naml: 15]. The meaning of the verse is that its being in the breast of the Prophet ﷺ is the state of every part of the Qur'an at the time of its revelation. When it is revealed, it is possible that the scribes would write it down. The Prophet ﷺ had indeed appointed a scribe for the revelation, so they would sometimes write down the verse at the time it was revealed, as the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit concerning His saying, ﴿Those who sit [at home] among the believers, other than those with a harm﴾ [al-Nisa': 95], indicates. Likewise, after its revelation it becomes recited, so what is negated is that it was recited before its revelation. This is what the context of the retraction requires, regarding the Prophet ﷺ reciting a book before this Qur'an, such that one might suppose that what he brought of the Qur'an was something he had been reciting earlier. When that was negated, it was fitting to disclose the state of receiving the Qur'an, and that is the position of His saying, ﴿in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge﴾, as He said, ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193], and He said, ﴿Thus, that We may strengthen your heart by it﴾ [al-Furqan: 32].

As for the information that it is clear signs, that is a preparation for the purpose and a completion of its requirement. For this reason, the more apt view is that the prepositional phrase in His saying, ﴿in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge﴾, is a second predicate for the pronoun. The reading fits as follows: "You did not recite any book before it, nor did you write it with your right hand; rather, it was cast into your breast, and it is clear signs."

It is also permissible that what is meant by the breasts of those who have been given knowledge is the breasts of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and the memorisers among the Muslims. In that case, His saying, ﴿in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge﴾ serves as a completion of the praise of the Qur'an, and the purpose is the information that the Qur'an is clear signs. Then the prepositional phrase is an adjective of "signs", and the retraction is confined to His saying, ﴿Rather, it is clear signs﴾.

The clause ﴿And none deny Our signs except the wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) indicating that the polytheists denied the signs of the Qur'an despite the clarity of their indication that they are from Allah, because they are wrongdoers who have no fairness. The attribute of wrongdoers is to deny the truth, and the inclination of their souls toward wrongdoing leads them to deny it, as He said, ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. So they are deeply immersed in wrongdoing, as was previously stated in describing them as disbelievers and falsifiers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 50:

﴿And they say, "Why were no signs sent down upon him from his Lord?" Say, "The signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."﴾

When he had mentioned the deniers of the sign of the Qur'an three times, and described them as disbelievers, falsifiers and wrongdoers, the discourse moved on to their statement arising from their denial. That statement is their request that the Prophet bring visible signs that break the customary order, which would demonstrate that Allah created them as confirmation of the Messenger, just as He created the she-camel of Salih and the staff of Musa. This is part of their coarseness: they are only moved by matters that are witnessed, and they assume that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, sets himself up to oppose them. So they propose to him what they desire, in order to make the extraordinary things they ask for into a topic of gatherings, so that the presence of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, among them would be like the presence of charlatans and owners of tricks (al-khanqatarat). I have already presented the explanation of this delusion at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why was no sign sent down upon him from his Lord?"﴾ [al-An'am: 37] in Surah al-An'am.

The meaning of "with Allah" (ʿinda Allah) is that the signs are from the work of power which proceeds according to His will, exalted is He. Because they are dependent upon His will, they are likened to a thing kept safe with its owner.

The restrictive particle "innama" (only) confines the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to the attribute of warning, that is, the messengership, and does not extend it to creating signs or proposing them to his Lord. It is a restriction of exclusion (qasr ifrad), in reply to their claim that it is right for one described as a messenger to bring visible extraordinary things.

The meaning is: it is not conceded that conveying the message requires bringing extraordinary things according to the desire and proposal of the people, such that they would be excused for not believing the Messenger if he did not bring them a sign according to their proposal.

From the circumstances of the message, only the attribute of warner is singled out for mention, as an allusion to the polytheists that their condition calls for warning, which is the anticipation of harm.

"Mubin" (clear): one who makes the warning clear through rational proofs that indicate the truth of what he reports.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read "ayat" (plural), while Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim and Khalaf read "ayah" (singular). The plural and singular are equivalent here, because the intent is the genus, and a single sign is sufficient for confirmation.

﴿Do they not find it sufficient that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them? Surely in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe.﴾

This is a continuation of the verse ﴿Say: The signs are only with God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 50], and it is an ascent in the argument.

The interrogative is one of wonder and denial. The meaning is: Is it not sufficient for them, among the signs, the signs of the Qur'an? Every measure of its inimitability (i'jaz) is a sign of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ. The Qur'an contains about six thousand verses, and the measure of every three verses is an inimitable measure. Thus the Qur'an contains the equivalent of two thousand miracles, and this has not been granted to any of God's messengers.

"Al-Kitab" means the Qur'an. The word "the Book" is used instead of "the Qur'an," which functions almost as a proper name for it, because the familiar term "al-Kitab" points to the meaning of its exaltation: that it is the most renowned among the books of the prophets.

The clause ﴿which is recited to them﴾ is either a new independent clause or a circumstantial clause (hal), because the Book is well known and does not need a qualifier, as the root of the word "recitation" (tilawa) suggests spread and currency.

The present tense was chosen over a descriptive form such as "recited to them" (matluwwan 'alayhim), because the present tense indicates continuity. Thus the root of yutla and the form of the present tense together indicate the generality of places and times.

[p. 15]

The phrase ﴿which is recited to them﴾ and what follows point to five distinctions of the Qur'an over other miracles.

The first distinction: what is indicated by ﴿which is recited to them﴾ is the spread of its inimitability and its generality in assemblies, regions and different eras, such that the perception of its inimitability is not restricted to a particular group in a particular time, unlike the manifest miracles such as the staff of Moses, the she-camel of Salih, and the healing of the blind. The Qur'an is recited, and within its recitation are verses that challenge people to match it and that have recorded their incapacity to match it before they attempted it. So it was as it said. It is therefore a lasting miracle, whereas the other miracles are transient miracles.

The second distinction: that it is something recited. This is higher than the other miracles being visible states, because perceiving the recited is an intellectual, reflective perception, which is higher than sensory perceptions. Thus the miracle of the Qur'an is more fitting for the ages of knowledge that humanity would later reach.

The third distinction: what is indicated by ﴿Surely in that is mercy﴾. This clause is presented as a justification, to express wonder at their not being satisfied with the Book. The justification completes what the expression "the Book" and "which is recited to them" imply. The demonstrative ﴿that﴾ refers to the Book, so that it is recalled with all its attributes, and to highlight it with the exaltation that the demonstrative implies. The indefinite "mercy" (rahma) is for magnification, meaning its worth cannot be measured.

The recited Book thus contains what is mercy for them in the way a container contains its contents, because it includes the establishment of the Law (shari'a), which is mercy and welfare for people in their worldly life. The Qur'an, together with being a miracle that indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ and guides to believing him like other miracles, is also a means of knowledge, legislation and manners for those to whom it is recited. By this it surpasses the other miracles, which only establish the truthfulness of the messenger who brings them.

The fourth distinction: what is indicated by ﴿and a reminder﴾. The Qur'an contains admonitions, warnings, and information about the consequences of deeds, and preparation for the second life, and similar things that are a reminder, in whose remembrance is the good of both abodes. By this it surpasses the other silent miracles, which convey nothing more than that the one who comes with them is truthful.

[p. 16]

The fifth distinction: that the Qur'an being a recited book whose distinctive features can be perceived by every Arab, and by every non-Arab who has mastered Arabic, such as the leading grammarians, distances it from resembling the incantations of sorcerers and talismans. No detractor can claim that it is imaginings, as the people of Pharaoh said to Moses: ﴿O sorcerer﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 49]. God also said, relating about the polytheists when they saw the miracle of the splitting of the moon: ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "Continuous magic"﴾ [al-Qamar: 2]. His words "they turn away" indicate that this statement came from them regarding a visible miracle.

Joined to mercy and reminder is the phrase ﴿for a people who believe﴾, to indicate that these benefits from the Qur'an exceed those found in the other miracles, namely the benefit of believing in what the Messenger ﷺ brought.

These are therefore great distinctions of the miracle of the Qur'an, present both in the presence of the Messenger ﷺ and in his absence, and independent of the need for his explanation and completion through preaching and repetition of it.

Mentioning the believers by the title "a people who believe," rather than saying "for the believers," indicates that faith is among the constituents of their peoplehood; that is, for a people whose emblem is to believe, meaning a people whose emblem is reflection and fairness. When the evidences of faith are established for them, they believe, and they do not obstinately resist out of injustice and arrogance. The verb is intended to denote a state close to the future. In it is also an indirect reference to those who were not satisfied with his miracle and proposed other signs with which it has no comparison.

[Page 17]

After He had silenced them with the decisive proof, he was commanded to make Allah the judge between himself and them, since their denial persisted despite the conclusive evidence.

This is speech of fairness, its purpose being to draw the addressee on gently.

﴿Kafá billāh﴾ (Allah is sufficient) means: He is sufficient for me in making the truth manifest. The bāʾ (ba) is redundant (zāʾidah), for emphasis. A parallel to it has already occurred in His words: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 4:79], in Surat al-Nisāʾ.

[Page 18 continues below]

*Al-shahīd* (the witness) means *al-shāhid* (the one who witnesses). Since it implies the meaning of *al-ḥākim* (the judge), it takes the adverbial phrase *bayni wa baynakum* (between me and you). Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah said about the king ʿAmr ibn Hind:

He is the Lord and the Witness over the day of al-Ḥiyārayn, and the affliction is an affliction.

The clause ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ confirms the meaning of being sufficient with Him as witness, so it functions in relation to it as an emphasis.

﴿And those who believed in falsehood and disbelieved in Allah, they are the losers﴾. After He had dealt fairly with them by saying ﴿Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you﴾, He continued in fairness, with something they cannot deny: that those who hold falsehood to be true and disbelieve in Allah are the losers in the judgment and the matter committed to Allah, the Exalted. If they reflect truly on their belief in Allah, they will find themselves not believing in His divinity, since they have associated with Him what is not truly worthy of divinity. Thus they know that they have disbelieved in Allah, and it is therefore determined that they believed in falsehood. The speech is thus directed in the manner of His words: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Saba 34:24], and the words of Ḥassān about Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb in the days of his jāhiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance):

Would you satirize him, when you are not his equal? So your evil is for your good, the ransom.

In the juxtaposition of *āmanū* (they believed) and *kafarū* (they disbelieved) there is an embellishment of opposition, which is *ṭibāq* (antithesis).

*Al-bāṭil* (falsehood) is the opposite of *al-ḥaqq* (truth), i.e., that which is not worthy of being believed in, meaning that which is not a true god, yet they ascribe divinity to it. That is their belief in the divinity of idols. As for their disbelief in Allah, it is because they associated partners with Him in divinity, thereby disbelieving in His greatest attribute, which is oneness (*waḥdāniyyah*).

The demonstrative (*ism al-ishārah*, "those") serves to draw attention to the fact that those indicated are deserving of the judgment stated after the demonstrative, on account of the attributes mentioned for them before it, like His words: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:5].

The restriction (*qaṣr*, exclusive limitation) derived from the definiteness of both parts of the nominal sentence ﴿they are the losers﴾ is a figurative restriction (*qaṣr idiʿāʾī*), for the sake of exaggeration in their being characterized by a great loss, to the extent that every other loss compared with their loss is as nothing;

[Page 18]

so it is as if they alone were the ones who lost. Thus the compound expression that conveys the restriction of loss to them is used. That is because the great, everlasting wretchedness has become binding upon them.

The word *al-khusrān* (loss) is borrowed metaphorically (*istuʿīra*) for the frustration of the hoped-for outcome of toilsome labor, by analogy with the state of one who toils in trade to gain wealth, but then loses his capital. It has already been mentioned at His words: ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:16].
