It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿And they say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 50], as a thorough refutation of their doubts and an annulment of the pretexts for their turning away, which arise from obstinacy, although they imagine that they turned away only because they were not convinced of the truth of the Messenger's sign (ﷺ).

The reason for its placement here is that, when their disbelief in God was mentioned, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) was warning them of punishment for it, and they were seeking to hasten it, He mentioned their mockery of it immediately after mentioning disbelief. "Seeking to hasten the punishment" (istiʿjāl al-ʿadhāb) means asking for it to come sooner, namely the punishment with which they had been threatened, and their purpose in this was to belittle the threat. The construction ﴿they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ was discussed earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if God were to hasten evil for people as they seek to hasten good﴾ [Yunus: 11] in Surat Yunus, and in His saying: ﴿They ask you to hasten evil before good﴾ [al-Raʿd: 6] in Surat al-Raʿd. The definite article in "al-ʿadhāb" is the definite article of the genus (taʿrīf al-jins).

Their seeking the punishment is related in the present tense (bi-ṣīghat al-muḍāriʿ) to evoke the state of their seeking it, for the purpose of expressing wonder at it, as in His saying: ﴿He argues with us concerning the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 74].

He nullified what they intended by His saying: ﴿Were it not for a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them﴾. That is because the descent of punishment is not in the hand of the Messenger (peace be upon him), nor does it follow their demand and their impatience. Rather, God is the one who determines the time of its descent upon them, at a term He decreed by His knowledge.

[Page 19 marker.] The word "specified" (musammā) is meant as "determined and limited," that is, in God's knowledge, exalted is He. It has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And We cause to remain in the wombs what We will for a specified term﴾ [al-Hajj: 5] in Surat al-Hajj.

The meaning is: Were it not for the determined term appointed for the descent of the punishment upon them, the punishment would have come upon them immediately, because their disbelief deserves the hastening of their punishment. But God willed to delay it for wisdoms He knew, among them giving them respite so that whoever among them would believe after the threat might believe, and so that they would know that God is not provoked by their seeking the punishment, because He is All-Wise, who does not contravene what He has decreed by His wisdom, and All-Forbearing, who gives His servants respite. So the meaning is: Were it not for a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them at the time they sought to hasten it. Then He warned them that it would indeed come upon them suddenly, and that its coming is certain, as indicated by the lam of oath and the nun of emphasis, and that will be at the arrival of the term appointed for it. The punishment of the Day of Badr did indeed befall them suddenly, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Even if you had made an appointment, you would have differed concerning the appointment﴾ [al-Anfal: 42]. He uprooted their chieftains that day, and they were left regretful (wa-suqita fī aydīhim).

Since God had prepared for them a punishment greater than the punishment of the Day of Badr, namely the punishment of Hell, which encompasses all of them, He followed their warning of the punishment of the Day of Badr with a warning of the greater punishment. Their seeking the punishment is repeated for its sake, placed as a parenthetical between the two coordinated clauses, as an allusion that this is the answer to their seeking: they sought the punishment, so they were warned of two punishments, one of which is sooner than the other. In the repetition of ﴿they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ there is a threat and a warning of their being seized. Thus the clause ﴿And indeed Hell﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿and it will certainly come upon them suddenly﴾, so they are two punishments, as the apparent sense of the coordination requires.

Encompassing (al-iḥāṭa) is a metonymy (kināya) for their not escaping from it.

By "the disbelievers" is meant those who seek hastening. They are brought to mind by the description "disbelievers" to indicate that this is what makes the punishment encompass them. The active participle is used for future encompassing, although the active participle normally indicates attribution in the present time, by treating the future as if it were the present, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, since it comes from One whose report is not disputed.

﴿The day the punishment covers them﴾ is connected to "encompassing" (muḥīṭa), meaning: it encompasses them on the day the punishment covers them. In His saying: ﴿The punishment covers them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ there is a depiction of encompassing. Covering (al-ghashayān) means concealing and veiling.

[Page 20 marker.] His saying: ﴿from above them﴾ is an explanation of the covering, depicting it in order to magnify its condition, like His saying: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿam: 38], and as an emphasis of the meaning of covering to remove the possibility of figurative usage. It is thus in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the punishment, and it is an emphasizing circumstantial clause.

His saying: ﴿and from beneath their feet﴾ is a safeguard (iḥtirās) against what the covering might suggest of mere above-ness, meaning: a fire will strike them from beneath them, blazing toward them while they are above it. Since it is coordinated with the circumstantial clause by the conjunction "wa", and since it is not suitable to be a restriction on "yaghshāhum" (because covering implies above-ness), it became necessary to posit a verb to which "from beneath their feet" is attached, namely that a deleted governing verb be assumed. This action has been counted among the particularities of the conjunction "wa" in coordination: that it coordinates a deleted governing verb whose complement indicates it, as in the saying of ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zibaʿrā:

Would that your husband had become one girding on a sword and a spear.

He means: and holding a spear, since a spear is not girded. It is possible for it to be an object of accompaniment (maʿiyya). Abū ʿUbayda, al-Aṣmaʿī, al-Jurmī, al-Yazīdī, and those who agree with them consider this to be of the type of "tadmīn" (implicit inclusion of meaning), that a verb is given the meaning of another verb suitable to be attached to what is mentioned. So in this verse, the verb "yaghshāhum" is assumed to include the meaning of "yuṣībuhum" (strikes them) or "yaʾkhudhuhum" (seizes them). The intended purpose of this is a metonymy for the punishment encompassing them. For this reason the two sides, right and left, were not mentioned, because the purpose of the metonymy has already been achieved.

The context is one of concision (ījāz), because it is a context of anger and threat, unlike His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and behind them and from their right and from their left﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 17], because that is a narration of Satan's insistence in whispering.

Nafiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read "yaqūlu" with the yāʾ (third person), and the pronoun refers to something known from the context. The implied meaning is: "and God says." The pronoun shifted from the first-person form, contrary to the apparent requirement, by way of iltifāt (shift of person), according to the view of many scholars of rhetoric. Or it is assumed: "and the angel charged over Hell says," or the meaning is: "and the punishment says," by God making the fire produce sounds as if it were the speech of one saying, "Taste!" Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar, and Yaʿqūb read it with the nūn, which is the nūn of majesty.

[Page 21 marker.] The meaning of ﴿what you used to do﴾ is: its recompense. Because the recompense corresponds in measure to what is recompensed, the name of the act was applied to it as a figurative usage, either a metonymy by the general relation (majāz mursal) or a figure by deletion (majāz bil-ḥadhf).

Rather, God is the one who determines the time of its descent upon them, at a term He decreed by His knowledge.

[Page 19 marker.] The word "specified" (musammā) is meant as "determined and limited," that is, in God's knowledge, exalted is He. It has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And We cause to remain in the wombs what We will for a specified term﴾ [al-Hajj: 5] in Surat al-Hajj.

The meaning is: Were it not for the determined term appointed for the descent of the punishment upon them, the punishment would have come upon them immediately, because their disbelief deserves the hastening of their punishment. But God willed to delay it for wisdoms He knew, among them giving them respite so that whoever among them would believe after the threat might believe, and so that they would know that God is not provoked by their seeking the punishment, because He is All-Wise, who does not contravene what He has decreed by His wisdom, and All-Forbearing, who gives His servants respite. So the meaning is: Were it not for a specified term, the punishment would have come upon them at the time they sought to hasten it. Then He warned them that it would indeed come upon them suddenly, and that its coming is certain, as indicated by the lam of oath and the nun of emphasis, and that will be at the arrival of the term appointed for it. The punishment of the Day of Badr did indeed befall them suddenly, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Even if you had made an appointment, you would have differed concerning the appointment﴾ [al-Anfal: 42]. He uprooted their chieftains that day, and they were left regretful (wa-suqita fī aydīhim).

Since God had prepared for them a punishment greater than the punishment of the Day of Badr, namely the punishment of Hell, which encompasses all of them, He followed their warning of the punishment of the Day of Badr with a warning of the greater punishment. Their seeking the punishment is repeated for its sake, placed as a parenthetical between the two coordinated clauses, as an allusion that this is the answer to their seeking: they sought the punishment, so they were warned of two punishments, one of which is sooner than the other. In the repetition of ﴿they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾ there is a threat and a warning of their being seized. Thus the clause ﴿And indeed Hell﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿and it will certainly come upon them suddenly﴾, so they are two punishments, as the apparent sense of the coordination requires.

Encompassing (al-iḥāṭa) is a metonymy (kināya) for their not escaping from it.

By "the disbelievers" is meant those who seek hastening. They are brought to mind by the description "disbelievers" to indicate that this is what makes the punishment encompass them. The active participle is used for future encompassing, although the active participle normally indicates attribution in the present time, by treating the future as if it were the present, to draw attention to the certainty of its occurrence, since it comes from One whose report is not disputed.

﴿The day the punishment covers them﴾ is connected to "encompassing" (muḥīṭa), meaning: it encompasses them on the day the punishment covers them. In His saying: ﴿The punishment covers them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ there is a depiction of encompassing. Covering (al-ghashayān) means concealing and veiling.

[Page 20 marker.] His saying: ﴿from above them﴾ is an explanation of the covering, depicting it in order to magnify its condition, like His saying: ﴿nor any bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿam: 38], and as an emphasis of the meaning of covering to remove the possibility of figurative usage. It is thus in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the punishment, and it is an emphasizing circumstantial clause.

His saying: ﴿and from beneath their feet﴾ is a safeguard (iḥtirās) against what the covering might suggest of mere above-ness, meaning: a fire will strike them from beneath them, blazing toward them while they are above it. Since it is coordinated with the circumstantial clause by the conjunction "wa", and since it is not suitable to be a restriction on "yaghshāhum" (because covering implies above-ness), it became necessary to posit a verb to which "from beneath their feet" is attached, namely that a deleted governing verb be assumed. This action has been counted among the particularities of the conjunction "wa" in coordination: that it coordinates a deleted governing verb whose complement indicates it, as in the saying of ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zibaʿrā:

Would that your husband had become one girding on a sword and a spear.

He means: and holding a spear, since a spear is not girded. It is possible for it to be an object of accompaniment (maʿiyya). Abū ʿUbayda, al-Aṣmaʿī, al-Jurmī, al-Yazīdī, and those who agree with them consider this to be of the type of "tadmīn" (implicit inclusion of meaning), that a verb is given the meaning of another verb suitable to be attached to what is mentioned. So in this verse, the verb "yaghshāhum" is assumed to include the meaning of "yuṣībuhum" (strikes them) or "yaʾkhudhuhum" (seizes them). The intended purpose of this is a metonymy for the punishment encompassing them. For this reason the two sides, right and left, were not mentioned, because the purpose of the metonymy has already been achieved.

The context is one of concision (ījāz), because it is a context of anger and threat, unlike His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and behind them and from their right and from their left﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 17], because that is a narration of Satan's insistence in whispering.

Nafiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read "yaqūlu" with the yāʾ (third person), and the pronoun refers to something known from the context. The implied meaning is: "and God says." The pronoun shifted from the first-person form, contrary to the apparent requirement, by way of iltifāt (shift of person), according to the view of many scholars of rhetoric. Or it is assumed: "and the angel charged over Hell says," or the meaning is: "and the punishment says," by God making the fire produce sounds as if it were the speech of one saying, "Taste!" Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar, and Yaʿqūb read it with the nūn, which is the nūn of majesty.

[Page 21 marker.] The meaning of ﴿what you used to do﴾ is: its recompense. Because the recompense corresponds in measure to what is recompensed, the name of the act was applied to it as a figurative usage, either a metonymy by the general relation (majāz mursal) or a figure by deletion (majāz bil-ḥadhf).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 56:

﴿O My servants who have believed, indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone.﴾

It is an initiating resumptive clause (isti'naf ibtida'i) that falls as a parenthetical interjection between two coordinated clauses: the clause ﴿But those who believed in falsehood and disbelieved in Allah — those are the losers﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 52], and the clause ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds — We will surely settle them in lofty chambers of Paradise﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 58] and what follows. This is a command to emigrate from the land of disbelief. Its connection to what precedes it is that when Allah mentioned the obstinacy of the polytheists regarding the confirmation of the Qur'an and the mention of the faith of the People of the Book in it, He gave permission to the believers among the people of Makkah to leave the abode of the deniers for the abode of those who affirm the Qur'an, namely the people of Madinah, for at that time they were a mix of Muslims and Jews. Thus the believers would be in their neighbourhood, safe from trials, worshipping their Lord without being tormented.

A group of the weak among the people of Makkah had believed in their hearts but were unable to manifest their faith out of fear of the polytheists, such as al-Harith ibn Rabi'ah ibn al-Aswad, as was mentioned earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10] at the beginning of this surah. They had an excuse, for they found no safe refuge away from the people of polytheism. And a group of the Muslims had been able to emigrate to Abyssinia earlier. When the people of Madinah embraced Islam, the excuse of the weak believers ceased, for it became within their capacity to emigrate to Madinah. Therefore Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed My earth is vast, so worship Me alone.﴾

His saying ﴿Indeed My earth is vast﴾ is a figurative, compound expression used to remind that there are lands in which the Muslim can dwell in safety. It is like the saying of Iyas ibn Qabisah al-Ta'i:

Did you not see that the earth is wide and spacious,
So will a single plot of its lands defeat me?

Do you not see how he grounded on its being wide his saying: "so will a single plot defeat me"? Likewise, in the verse He grounded on its being vast the command to worship Allah alone, for the purpose of leaving what the weak believers were being tried by, since they were being compelled to worship idols, as was mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who is forced while his heart remains firm in faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106].

So the meaning is: My earth in which you are safe from the polytheists is vast, and it is Madinah and the villages adjacent to it, such as Khaybar, al-Nadir, Qurayzah and Qaynuqa'. None of them became a place of safety except after the people of Madinah embraced Islam, because those villages were allies of the people of Madinah from the Aws and the Khazraj.

His saying ﴿so worship Me alone﴾ indicates that the reason for the command to them to emigrate is to enable them to manifest monotheism and establish the religion. This is the criterion for the obligation to emigrate from a land in which the Muslim is tried in his religion and in which non-Islamic rulings are applied.

The address with the definite construction by annexation (al-ta'rif bi'l-idafah) serves to honour the annexed term. The Qur'anic usage is that when ('ibad, servants) is annexed to the pronoun of majesty (Allah), it generally refers to the believers, unless there is an indicator, as in His saying: ﴿Did you lead astray these My servants?﴾ [al-Furqan: 17]. Accordingly, there is no qualification by ﴿who believed﴾ that would be needed, owing to what the relative clause implies, namely that they believed in Allah truly, but they were tried to the point of being compelled to show disbelief.

The fa' in His saying ﴿fa-iyya-ya﴾ is the fa' of consequence (fa' al-tafri'), while the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-'budun﴾ is either a fa' emphasizing the first fa' to indicate the confirmation of the consequence both in the act and in its object, meaning: "do not worship other than Me, so worship Me"; or it indicates an omitted verb governing the first-person pronoun, as an emphasis on the worship, the estimate being: "and worship Me alone, so worship Me." The latter is more suitable given the implication of fronting for exclusivity, since when it conveyed the command to restrict the worship to Him, mentioning the fa' was a sign of an estimated verb omitted, the purpose of whose estimation is emphasis. This was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿And of Me alone be in awe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40] at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The ya' of the first person was elided after the nun of protection (nun al-wiqayah) for lightness and for conformity with the rhyme (fasilah), and its parallels are numerous.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 57:

﴿Every soul shall taste death; then to Us you will be returned.﴾

This is a second interjected clause (i'tiraḍ, a parenthetical insertion) placed between the two conjoined sentences. Its purpose is to affirm the threat contained in the sentence ﴿And those who believe in falsehood…﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 52] to its end, and the promise contained in the sentence ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them in lofty chambers of Paradise﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 58]. That is: death overtakes all souls, and then they are returned to Allah.

Its purpose is also to make light of what the believers encounter of harm for the sake of Allah, even if it reaches the point of death, in comparison with what awaits them of Allah's bounty and His everlasting reward. It also contains a notice (iday) that they will face struggle (jihad) in the way of Allah.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read ﴿turja'un﴾ (تَرْجِعُونَ) with the taa' of address, considering it an address to the believers in His words ﴿O My servants who believe﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 56]. Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with the yaa' of the third person (يَرْجِعُونَ), following His words ﴿The punishment will envelop them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 29, verses 58–59:**

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds, We will surely settle them in the lofty chambers of Paradise, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. How excellent is the reward of those who work.﴾ ﴿Those who are patient and upon their Lord they rely.﴾

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon the clause ﴿Those who believe in falsehood﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 52].

The relative pronoun (*mawsul*) is used to indicate the reason for the statement of the predicate, meaning: We will settle them in chambers because of their faith and their righteous deeds.

*Al-tabwi'a* means to lodge and to settle. It has already been discussed under His saying, ﴿And We had certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement﴾ [Yunus: 93], in Surah Yunus.

The majority of reciters read ﴿*lanubawwi'annahum*﴾ with a single *ba'* after the *nun* of majesty and a *hamza* after the *waw*. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿*lanuthawwiyannahum*﴾ with a *tha'* after the *nun* and a *ya'* after the *waw*, from *athwa*, with the *hamza* of causation, when he makes him *thawi* (dwelling), meaning residing in a place.

*Al-ghuraf* is the plural of *ghurfah*, which is a room raised above others. It was discussed under His saying, ﴿Those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber﴾ [Al-Furqan: 75], at the end of Surah al-Furqan.

The clause ﴿How excellent is the reward of those who work﴾ and so on is an expression of praise and admiration for the reward they were given; therefore it is separated from the conjunction.

His saying, ﴿Those who are patient﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, following common usage, and the estimated meaning is: ﴿they are﴾ those who are patient. What is meant is their patience in upholding the religion and bearing the harm of the polytheists, while knowing that they would encounter it. So they relied upon their Lord, did not care about the severing of ties by their people or their deprivation of their wealth, and then they left their homelands, fleeing with their religion from trials.

Among the subtle points is the contrast between the punishment covering the disbelievers from above them and from beneath their feet, and the blessing covering the believers from above them with the chambers and from beneath them with the rivers.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase ﴿upon their Lord﴾ before its governed element ﴿they rely﴾ is for emphasis.

The meaning of *tawakkul* (reliance) has already been explained under His saying, ﴿So when you have decided, then rely upon Allah﴾ [Al Imran: 159], in Surah Al Imran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 60:

﴿And how many a creature there is that does not carry its provision; Allah provides for it, and for you. And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 57]. When Allah made the matter of death easy for them in the cause of Allah's good pleasure, and they were among those who did not care for death, He knew that they would say to themselves: "We do not fear death, but we fear poverty and the loss of livelihood." The Arabs' disregard for death was a natural disposition (sajiyyah) among them, just as fear of disgrace (khashyat al-maʿarrah) was one of their dispositions, as we explained at the words of His, exalted is He: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 31]. So He followed that by reminding them that their provision is upon Allah and that He will not waste them. He set for them the example of the provision of animals, and for the appropriateness of His words ﴿Indeed, My earth is spacious﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 56], concerning the expectation of those who emigrate from Makkah that they would not find provision in the lands to which they emigrate. It is also appropriate because it comes after the mention of trust in God (tawakkul) in His words ﴿and upon their Lord they rely﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 59]. And in the hadith: "If you were to rely upon Allah with the reliance due to Him, you would be provided for as the bird is provided for: it goes out hungry in the morning and returns full in the evening."

Perhaps what is in this verse and in the hadith is directed at the first believers. Allah guaranteed them their provision because of their trust in Him when they left their wealth in Makkah for the emigration to Allah and His Messenger, and their trust was the true trust (ḥaqq al-tawakkul), that is, its most complete and most prudent form. No one places himself at this level who has not done what they did.

Page 25
The discussion of kaʾayyin (how many) has already been presented at the words of His, exalted is He: "And how many a prophet has fought, with him many devoted ones (rabbiyyūn)" in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

His words ﴿And how many a creature there is that does not carry its provision﴾ are a statement not intended to convey a ruling; rather it is used figuratively and in compound form for its implied meaning, which is the argument for guaranteeing the provision of the trusting believers. Its illustration, for the sake of approximation, is the guarantee of provision for the many animals that roam the earth and do not carry their provision, namely the wild grazing beasts. The indicator of this usage is His words ﴿Allah provides for it, and for you﴾, which is a explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī) clarifying the reason this statement was brought; for this reason He conjoined "and for you" to the pronoun in "creature" (dābbah). The purpose is the illustration in facilitation and inspiration toward the means that lead to provision, even though the means of provision differ.

The word "carry" (ḥaml) in His words ﴿does not carry its provision﴾ may be used in its literal sense, meaning they go forth not carrying their provision, unlike caravan beasts that carry their provision, which is their fodder, upon their backs; rather they go forth eating from the plants of the earth. It may also be used figuratively for the bearing of burden (takalluf) for it, as in the verse of Jarir:

You were laden with a great matter, so you bore it with patience.

That is, they do not burden themselves for their provision. This is the condition of most animals except the ant and the mouse; it is said also some birds such as the magpie.

The fronting of the subject before the verbal predicate in His words ﴿Allah provides for it﴾, rather than saying "provides for it Allah," serves to convey the sense of exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ): that is, Allah alone provides for it, not another. Hence why would you worship idols that hold no provision in their hand?

The clause ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Allah provides for it, and for you﴾. The meaning: Allah provides for you, and He is the All-Hearing of your supplication, the All-Knowing of what is in your souls of sincerity to Allah in your deeds, your trust, and your hope from Him for provision.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 61:

Page 26
﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?", they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾
This statement relates back to His saying: ﴿And those who believe in falsehood and disbelieve in Allah - those are the losers﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 52], as a wonder at the contradictions of their disbelief. That is, they disbelieve in Allah, yet if someone asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would acknowledge that Allah is the Creator of that, and they do not ascribe to their idols any share of creation. So how does this accord with their claim of divinity for their idols? For this reason Allah said, ﴿Then how are they deluded?﴾, meaning: how are they turned away from the Oneness of Allah and from abandoning their associating with Him that which creates nothing?

This reproach is based on the fact that when they are asked they cannot do otherwise than acknowledge, because that is indeed the reality; and because the Qur'an is recited to them whenever something relating to them is revealed, and the Muslims recite it in their hearing. So if they were able to deny what was attributed to them, they would have voiced it.

The pronoun of the plural absent (third person) refers to those who believe in falsehood, disbelieve in Allah and seek to hasten the punishment, by the indication of His saying: ﴿Then how are they deluded?﴾

The interrogation in His saying ﴿Then how are they deluded?﴾ is one of denial and wonder.

The specific mention of the subjection of the sun and the moon from among the manifestations of the creation of the heavens and the earth is because of what their movement contains of evidence of great power, together with the favour upon people in that He tied the times of night and day and the regulation of months and seasons to their movement.

The subjection (taskhir) of a thing means compelling it to a severe task. I think it is literal, whether the one subjected (al-musakhkhar, with fatha) possesses will or is an inanimate object.

This has already been discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], in Surat al-A'raf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 62:

[Page 27]
﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants, and restricts it for him. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

This is another argument against them, to refute their polytheism and expose the contradiction in their position. For they used to acknowledge that the Provider is Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth, or who owns hearing and sight?"﴾ [Yunus: 31], up to His saying: ﴿They will say, "Allah." So say, "Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ [Yunus: 31] in Surah Yunus. The style of this argument differs from the style of the one before it and the one after it, so He turned away from the structure of "And if you asked them" (wa la'in sa'altahum) as a variety of styles, to renew the listener's attention.

Woven into the argument for His sole right to provision is a reminder that He, the Exalted, gives provision to His servants according to His will, as evidence that He is the one who chooses in His disposal, and that this is not according to the measure of their needs, nor according to what appears to be benefit from what they are provided with.

Bast al-rizq (extending provision) means increasing it, and qadr (restricting) means reducing it. The intended meaning is that He is the Provider in all conditions of provision. This was already mentioned in His saying: ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26] in Surah al-Ra'd.

This verse thus follows the pattern of His saying in Surah al-Rum: ﴿Have they not seen that Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts? Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ [al-Rum: 37]. It combined the pronoun of the polytheists at its beginning with the fact that the signs are for the believers at its end.

The placing of the predicate-subject (musnad ilayhi) before the verbal predicate in His saying ﴿Allah extends provision﴾ serves to indicate exclusivity, meaning: Allah alone, not other than Him, extends provision and restricts it.

The use of the present tense (al-mudari') indicates the continual renewal of extending and restricting.

The addition of "for him" (lahu) after "and restricts" in this verse, unlike the verse in Surah al-Ra'd and the verse in Surah al-Qasas, is for an allusion, directing the believers who were tested in their wealth by the aggression of the polytheists against it, as indicated by His saying just before: ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 60], that this restriction in provision is for them and not against them, because of the reward and elevation of ranks that results for them from it. So in this purpose the side of the believers was given precedence. For this reason, "yaqdiru" was not followed by the preposition "ʿalā" (upon), as the meaning of qadr would require,

[Page 28]
as in His saying: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted for him, let him spend from what Allah has given him﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]. Some exegetes said: the polytheists reproached the Muslims for poverty, and it was said that some of the Muslims said: "If we emigrate, we will not find what we can spend."

The pronoun governed by the preposition "li" (for) refers back to "whom He wills of His servants," given that "whom He wills" is general and not a specific person, especially since its generality was clarified by His saying "of His servants." The meaning is: He extends provision to one group and restricts it for another group.

The concluding statement with His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ serves to indicate that all of that proceeds according to a wisdom that people do not perceive, and that Allah knows the patience of the patient and the impatience of the impatient, as was mentioned in His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿So Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3]. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿You will surely be tested in your wealth and your persons, and you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with Allah much harm. But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Al 'Imran: 186].

Ibn ʿĀshūr's commentary (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 29, verse 63:

﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and thereby gives life to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "God."﴾

The question-and-answer form is repeated so that the proofs stay closely linked to one another. The polytheists did not claim that their idols send down rain, as the verse makes clear. Therefore the argument was established against them, and they did not deny it while it struck their ears.

Included in the argument for God's sole power to send down rain is the fact that God gives life to the earth after its death. Although most polytheists attribute effects to their ordinary causes, as explained in the discussion of the two kinds of metaphor, the intellectual (*al-ḥaqīqa al-ʿaqliyya*, the attribution of an act to what is apparently its agent) and the metaphorical (*al-majāz al-ʿaqlī*), in their saying, "The spring made the herbs grow," the intellectual attribution is a true statement in the speech of the people of polytheism. This is because, despite this, they do not attribute the growing of plants to their idols. They have also acknowledged that the cause of growth, which is rain, is sent down from God. Therefore it follows for them that the growing of plants comes from God under every assumption.

In this embedded argument there is an approximate proof for the resurrection, as he (Ibn ʿĀshūr) said: "Look, then, at the traces of God's mercy, how He gives life to the earth after its death; indeed, that is the One who gives life to the dead, and He is capable of all things." He also said: ﴿And He gives life to the earth after its death; and thus you will be brought forth﴾ [al-Rūm: 19].

Since the context here is one of affirmation, the situation calls for emphasis through the addition of *min* (مِن) in the phrase ﴿min baʿdi mawtihā﴾ ("after its death"). This forces them to acknowledge that the one who does this is God and not their idols. For this reason there is no such requirement for adding *min* in the verse of al-Baqara, nor in the verse of al-Jāthiya: ﴿fa-aḥyā bihi al-arḍa baʿda mawtihā﴾ [al-Jāthiya: 5].

The phrase ﴿min baʿdi mawtihā﴾ also refers to the death of the earth, that is, the death of its vegetation, which occurs when rain is withheld from it during the seasons of drought or in years of barrenness. This is because He (God) paired it with the sending down of rain, by His will to give life to the earth, in His words ﴿fa-aḥyā bihi al-arḍa﴾. So it is certain that its death is by God's decree, since it is known that the earth's death followed a life that had preceded it of the same kind as this life. Thus the verse indicates that He is the one who disposes of the giving of life to the earth and its causing to die. From it is also known that He gives life to animals and causes them to die, by the method of *laḥn al-khiṭāb* (implicit meaning of discourse, drawing a conclusion from what is not explicitly stated).

Thus there is united, from these verses beginning with His words ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?"﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 61] up to here, the fundamentals of God's attributes of action, which are: creation, provision, giving life, and causing to die. For this reason, God commanded His Prophet ﷺ, after them, to praise Him with a statement that indicates the restriction of praise to Him.

* * *

﴿Say, "Praise be to God." But most of them do not understand.﴾

Since the proof against the polytheists became clear, that God alone is the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life and the Causer of death, and it follows from this that their idols have no share in these acts, which are the foundations of the order of all existing things on earth, this made it necessary to refute their polytheism with what they cannot deny or interpret away, after its proofs had struck their ears while they remained silent, showing no denial. From this follows the truthfulness of the Messenger, peace be upon him, in what he called them to, and their falsehood in what they boasted of against him concerning the command of God and His Messenger. Hence the command to praise Him for having granted him victory through proof, a victory that indicates He will also grant him victory by force. That is a great blessing deserving that God be praised for it, since He is the One who taught it to His Messenger ﷺ through His Book, while he did not know what the Book was or what faith was.

So this praise commanded here has an omitted complement, whose implied meaning is: "Praise be to God for that," that is, for the proofs mentioned earlier. It is not specific to the proof of the sending down of water from the sky. Such is the case with qualifiers that come after several clauses: they refer back to all of them, and their related elements (the *mutaʿallaqāt*, with the *lām* in the form *mutaʿallaqāt*, meaning the things they relate to) refer back with them. The context is like a fire on a hill (a clear indicator). Do you not see that each of those proofs deserves that God be praised for establishing it? Therefore the praise is not limited to the proof of the sending down of rain. Indeed, He, exalted is He, said in Surah Luqmān: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "God." Say, "Praise be to God." But most of them do not know﴾ [Luqmān: 25]. Therefore the statement ﴿Say, "Praise be to God"﴾ is not to be considered a parenthetical interjection (*iʿtirāḍ*).

As for ﴿bal aktharuhum lā yaʿqilūn﴾ ("but most of them do not understand"), the *bal* (بَلْ) here is a *iḍrāb intiqāl* (a transitional "but," moving from one topic to another): it shifts from praising God for the clarity of the proofs to censuring the polytheists, in that most of them are not alert to the force of these clear proofs. It is as if they had no intellect, because the clarity of proofs requires that every person with a measure of intelligence should perceive their conclusions. So they were treated as though they had no minds.

The attribution of the lack of intellect to most of them, rather than to all of them, is because among their intelligent and perceptive people there were some to whom those proofs became clear. Among them were those who believed, and among them were those who persisted in disbelief out of obstinacy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 64:

﴿And this worldly life is nothing but amusement and play. Indeed, the Hereafter, that is the [true] life, if they only knew.﴾

This statement is addressed to the two groups included in His saying: ﴿But most of them do not reason﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 63]. Their intelligent ones preferred the falsehood of this world over the truth that had become clear to them, while their common folk were aware of nothing beyond worldly affairs, and all of them denied resurrection. So God, after clarifying for them the proofs, drew their attention to the fact that the worldly life is like an illusion, and that the second life is the true life. By "life" is meant what it contains of conditions, and this extends to life itself.

[Page 31]

Al-lahw (amusement) is what people amuse themselves with, that is, what they occupy themselves with to escape troubling matters, or what they use to fill their free time that is empty of work. Al-la'ib (play) is what is intended for jest and frivolity. The explanation of play and amusement, and the reason why the worldly life is restricted to them, has already been given at His saying: ﴿And the worldly life is nothing but play and amusement﴾ [al-An'am: 32] in Surat al-An'am.

The restriction (al-hasr) here is claimed (ad-di'a'i), as previously explained.

This verse adds something by directing the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) to "this life," which is a demonstrative of contempt and disregard, like the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim, pointing to death:

"When this death comes, it will not find a need of mine
except that I have fulfilled its need."

In Surat al-An'am the demonstrative was not directed at the life. The reason is that the verse there did not contain anything that calls for belittling life, so the demonstrative was brought to convey its belittlement. As for the verse of Surat al-An'am, His saying preceded it: ﴿Until when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they will say, "O our regret over what we neglected concerning it"﴾ [al-An'am: 31]. In that verse He mentioned to them what will become apparent to them when the Hour comes: that their worldly life will have gone by in vain.

As for the mention of amusement (lahw) first here, and play (la'ib) in Surat al-An'am, the reason is that the verse of Surat al-An'am did not include a demonstrative intended to belittle the worldly life. So it began with "it is play," pointing to its belittlement, because play is more intense in its lack of benefit than amusement.

Since in this verse the Hereafter was pointed to in His saying: ﴿He gives life to the earth after its death﴾, He further clarified that the Hereafter is the true life. So for it was formed the pattern fi'lan (al-Hayawan), which is a form that indicates the meaning of movement, to clarify the meaning of the perfection of life to the degree commonly known. Movement and agitation are indications of the strength of vitality in a thing, like boiling and blazing.

They were ignorant of the Hereafter from its very root; therefore He said: ﴿if they only knew﴾. The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, and its indication is what preceded, or it is the answer placed first.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verses 65–66:

[Page 32]
﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them, and so that they may enjoy themselves; but they will come to know.﴾

The fa' (fa, "so/then") indicates that what follows is a consequence of what precedes it. The thing it is a consequence of is omitted; it is not one particular one of the earlier reports, but rather the sum of what is indicated by the force of the discourse about them and what the fa' requires. The sense is: they, i.e., the polytheists, being as described in their heedlessness of the signs of divine oneness and their disregard of what in their own circumstances are signs acknowledging God through them, do not supplicate humbly except to God. So when they board the ship, they call upon God. Accordingly, the pronouns of the plural absent (third person) refer to the polytheists.

This is a transition to holding them to account for what their supplication implies, when they do not associate with God another deity, after holding them to account for the implications of their own acknowledgments. For they call upon their idols in matters of their affairs and seek their help, but when a terror befalls them, they turn in humble supplication to God.

The mention, in this verse and in many verses like those in Surat Yunus and Surat al-Isra', is specifically of the state of fear from the terror of the sea, because their journeys on land did not involve a fear that encompassed the whole journey. They travelled in caravans, with their weapons, and passed along paths they were accustomed to, so no general fear confronted them. As for their voyage at sea, they were terrified by its terror, and neither abundance of number nor strength of equipment repelled it from them. Thus they humbly supplicate God seeking deliverance, and perhaps at that time they do not call upon their idols.

As for the subjugation of creatures, they only hoped for it from God the Exalted. Moreover, fear would penetrate them when they boarded the sea, because of their scant understanding of sailing it, since most of their journeys were in deserts.

The construction of riding with the particle "fi" (in) has already been mentioned at His saying: ﴿And he said, "Board it"﴾ [Hud: 41] in Surat Hud. Al-ikhlas: purification and singling out.

Al-din: dealing/practice. Here it is meant as supplication, i.e., they called upon God without associating their idols with Him. His saying confirms this: ﴿But when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate others with Him.﴾

[Page 33]
The particle of sudden occurrence (fa-idha) is used to indicate that they hastened to associating others with God at the very moment of their arrival on land, i.e., they hurried to what they were accustomed to: visiting their idols and slaughtering for them. The suddenness is conventional, according to what the mooring on land and reaching their dwelling-places require; they would hasten to feed food upon returning from the journey.

The lam in "liyakfuru" is the lam of causation, the lam of kay, and it is connected to the verb yushrikun. Kufr here is not shirk, but ingratitude for blessings, by the indication of His saying: ﴿for what We have given them﴾, since ita' here means bestowal, and by the indication that it is a consequence stated after "yushrikun", so the cause differs from the effect; ingratitude for blessings is caused by association. For when they hastened to the matters of association, they began to deny the blessing. So the lam is a subsidiary metaphor: the effect is likened to the motivating cause, so the particle of causation is borrowed for it in place of the fa' of consequence.

As for the lam in His saying "wa-liyatamatta'u" with a kasra on the lam, it is the lam of causation in the reading of Warsh from Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub. Qalun from Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with sukun, so it is the lam of command. After the conjunction it may be either sukun or kasra. On this reading the command is used in the sense of threat, like His saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [Fussilat: 40], and it is the conjoining of the clause of threat to the clause ﴿But when He delivers them to the land﴾, etc., like His saying in Surat al-Rum: ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them; so enjoy yourselves, but you will come to know﴾ [al-Rum: 34].

Al-tamatta': benefiting for a short period of time.

The clause ﴿but they will come to know﴾ is a consequence of the threat with a warning.

This is a particular reminder to the people of Makkah, and they were singled out from among the polytheistic Arabs because the people of Makkah were an exemplar (qudwah) for all the tribes. Do you not see that most of the Arab tribes were waiting to see what would become of the people of Makkah? So when the people of Makkah embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest (Fath), the delegations (wufud) of the tribes came, openly declaring their Islam.

The sentence is conjoined (ma'tufah) to the sentence ﴿فَإذا رَكِبُوا في الفُلْكِ دَعَوُا اللَّهَ﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 65], in terms of what that sentence contained of their rebuke for ingratitude for the blessings of God the Exalted. For this reason, this sentence was followed by His saying: ﴿وبِنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ يَكْفُرُونَ﴾.

The interrogative is for denial (istifham inkari), and the blessing of the security of their land is treated as something visibly present, so He denied them for not seeing it. Thus His saying ﴿أنّا جَعَلْنا حَرَمًا آمِنًا﴾ is the object (maf'ul) of "yaraw".

The meaning of this verse is known from what preceded when discussing His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وقالُوا إنْ نَتَّبِعِ الهُدى مَعَكَ نُتَخَطَّفْ مِن أرْضِنا أوَلَمْ نُمَكِّنْ لَهم حَرَمًا آمِنًا﴾ [al-Qasas: 57] in Surat al-Qasas. The people of Makkah were in the midst of security (bahbuhah min al-amn), while the other tribes around Makkah and beyond it would raid one another, make war upon one another (yataghawarun), and plunder one another (yatanahabun), whereas the people of Makkah were secure, and no one attacked them despite their small number. So God reminded them of this blessing upon them.

Al-batil: it is shirk, as preceded at His saying: ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِالباطِلِ﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 52] in this surah. The blessing of God intended here is the genus (jins) of which their rescue from drowning is part, and what is other than it of the perceptible and well-known blessings, and of the hidden blessings whose greatness they would have grasped had they reflected, among them the blessing of the Muhammadan message.

The present tense (mudari') in the three places indicates the renewal (tajaddud) of the act.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 29, verse 68:

﴿Who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against Allah or denies the truth when it comes to him? Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾

When he (Allah) had completed the description of their conditions, which deserved condemnation, and of the disorder of their affairs, He followed it with a concluding statement (tadhyil) that gathers them together as being a fabrication against Allah and a denial of the truth. Then He recompensed them with the fullest recompense befitting their state, which is that the Fire is their abode.

The description of their state opens with an interrogation about the existence of a group that does greater wrong than those who fabricated against Allah and denied the truth. This directs the minds of the listeners toward searching whether they can find anyone more wrongful than them. When they have reflected well, surveyed the places where wrongdoing is found, and reviewed its categories, they become certain that there is no wrongdoing more severe than the wrongdoing of these people.

They were the most wrongful of wrongdoers because wrongdoing (zulm) is an assault on someone by depriving him of his right. More severe than depriving someone is that one deprives the one who deserves something of it and gives it to one who does not deserve it, and that one attributes to someone what is innocent of it. Entitlement and its absence may be established by customs (al-'awa'id), may be established by the rulings of the revealed laws (al-shara'i'), and may be established by the judgments of sound intellects, which is the highest level of establishment. The affairs of the people of polytheism rest upon fabrication against Allah, in that they negated from Him the attributes of divinity that are established by the evidence of reason, and affirmed for Him attributes and acts from which He is exempt, by the evidence of reason. They also rest upon denying the Messenger (ﷺ) and rejecting the proof of the miracle, which reason requires, and upon attributing to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, what is innocent of it, in the face of the testimony of reason and of the custom they knew of him, as slander and falsehood. Thus, by combining the two matters, they placed things in positions where they could not possibly belong, and so they were the most wrongful of people, because the impossibility of a thing is stronger than its mere non-occurrence.

The restriction of the fabrication by the circumstantial qualifier in His saying "a lie" (kadhiban) serves to intensify the monstrousness of the fabrication, because the name "lie" is well known in people's usage for its ugliness. The term "fabrication" (iftira') was chosen to indicate that they deliberately invent, with a deliberation that no doubt mixes with.

The restriction of their denial of the truth by His saying ﴿when it came to him﴾ serves to incorporate a censure of those who deny by denying the blessing of the truth being sent to them, a blessing they did not esteem at its true value. The custom of sensible people is to seek the truth and to travel in its pursuit, whereas these people had the truth come to them right before them, and they denied it.

Also, the temporal "lamma" (لَمّا) indicates that their denial occurred immediately upon the arrival of the truth, that is, without giving themselves a period for reflection.

The sentence ﴿Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the sentence ﴿Who does greater wrong than one who invents a lie against Allah?﴾ and a confirmation of it. This is because the sentence ﴿Who does greater wrong than one who invents against Allah…﴾ up to its end contains a general indication of a dreadful recompense awaiting them. So its explanation is given by the content of the sentence ﴿Is there not in Hell a dwelling for the disbelievers?﴾, and by its wording and arrangement it conveys their being established in the torment of Hell, since it is made their dwelling.

So "al-mathwa" (the dwelling) is the place of abiding (al-thawa'), and "al-thawa'" is a long stay and residence.

He linked this to the title "the disbelievers" to draw attention to their deserving that for the sake of their disbelief.

The definite article in "al-kafirin" (the disbelievers) is the definite article of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), meaning "these disbelievers," namely those who were mentioned earlier as having fabricated against Allah a lie and denied the truth. The apparent requirement would have been to use a pronoun referring to them, but it was changed to the apparent noun in order to bring them to mind with the attribute of disbelief.

The hamza in ﴿Is there not in Hell a dwelling?﴾ is the interrogative of affirmation (al-istifham al-taqriri). Its origin is either denial, by treating the one being affirmed as if he were a denier, so that his affirmation becomes more binding upon him, or it is an interrogation, and when it entered upon the negation it conveyed affirmation, because the denial of a negation is an affirmation of the negated, and this affirmation is used for affirmation by way of kinaya (implicature, indirect expression). This affirming use of the hamza is the most common use of interrogation with negation, and from it is the verse of Jarir:

Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts, and the most generous of the worlds in giving the wine-cup?

It does not admit any meaning other than affirmation, by the testimony of taste and by the suitability of the context of praising the Caliph. This affirmation is addressed to whoever hears this speech. The fact that Hell is their dwelling is made a matter settled and known, such that everyone who is asked about it acknowledges it. This is a kinaya for the certainty of the outcome, in the manner of indirect allusion (iyma' al-kinaya).

[page 35]

[page 36]

[Page 37]

The reproach and condemnation of the polytheists is concluded by praising the believers, to show the greater care for them. The condemnation of their enemies never lacks praise of the believers, because that increases the enemies' rage and humiliation.

﴿Those who strive in Us﴾ are the first believers, so the relative pronoun (al-ladhina) functions like a definite noun with the definite article of previous reference (lam al-'ahd). This striving is patience under trials and harm and repelling the plots of the enemy. It is what was mentioned at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And whoever strives, strives only for himself﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 6], since at that time there was no fighting (jihad al-qital), as you have already learned.

The relative pronoun was used to indicate that the connection (al-silah) is the cause of the predicate. The meaning of ﴿strive in Us﴾ is: strive seeking Our good pleasure and the religion We have chosen for them. The expression of place (al-zarfiyya) is figurative; it is said that it is a zarfiyya of causation (ta'lil), which gives the emphasis of causation.

Guidance (al-hidaya) is direction and success through inward facilitation and legal guidance; that is, ﴿We will surely increase them in guidance﴾. The ways of Allah (subul Allah) are the deeds that lead to His pleasure and reward, likened to the roads that lead to the abode of the noble, who honours his guest.

By "the doers of good" (al-muhsinin) is meant all who were doers of good, that is, doing good deeds was their distinguishing mark, and this is a general term. In it is a commendation of the believers, that they are counted among those who came before from the prophets and the righteous. This is more effective in establishing their success than if it had been said, "Then those are the doers of good," because illustrating with matters that are established and well known serves to confirm the meanings. For this reason, in the teaching of the prayer upon the Prophet (ﷺ) comes his saying: "As You sent prayers upon Ibrahim and upon the family of Ibrahim."

The "being with" (al-ma'iyya) here is figurative, meaning care and concern for them.

The sentence has the sense of a concluding statement (tadhyil) by what it contains of generality. It was introduced as a conjunction (ma'tuf) to show that what is important in bringing it is what it contains of the states of the believers. So it was joined to their other state, and it gives the tadhyil by the generality of its ruling.

In His saying ﴿We will surely guide them in Our ways﴾ there is an allusion to the facilitation of the path of emigration (hijra), for which they were preparing in the days when this surah was revealed.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Surat al-Rum

This surah is called Surat al-Rum in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, as in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Ibn 'Abbas and Niyar ibn Mukram al-Aslami, and it will come shortly in the commentary on the first verse of the surah. The reason for this is that the name of the Romans (al-Rum) is mentioned in it and is not mentioned in any other part of the Qur'an.

It is entirely Meccan by agreement, as related by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi. The author of al-Itqan did not mention it among the surahs disputed as to whether they are Meccan or Medinan, nor among some of its verses. al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that this surah was revealed on the day of Badr, which would make it Medinan according to him. Abu Sa'id said: When the day of Badr came, the Romans prevailed over the Persians, and that pleased the believers and they rejoiced at it, so there was revealed ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-Rum: 1], ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum: 2], up to His saying ﴿by the help of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 5]. He used to read "ghalabat" with a fatha on the lam. This is a view no one followed. He also read "wa hum min ba'di ghalabihim sa-yughlabun" in the passive form, and he attributed such a reading to 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar. Abu al-Su'ud interpreted it in his tafsir, taking from al-Kashshaf, as an allusion to the victory of the Muslims over the Romans. Abu al-Su'ud said: The Muslims defeated them at the battle of Mu'ta in the ninth year.

From Ibn 'Abbas: the polytheists liked that the people of Persia would prevail over the Romans, because they and the Persians were both people of idols. From al-Hasan al-Basri: the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening﴾ [al-Rum: 17], up to the end of the verse, is Medinan, based on the view that that verse refers to the five daily prayers. He holds that the five prayers were prescribed in Medina, and that what was obligatory before the Hijra was two rak'ahs at whatever time was easy for the Muslim. This is based on an anomaly.

It is the eighty-fourth surah in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Inshiqaq

[Page 40]
and before Surat al-'Ankabut. It has been related from Qatada and others that the Romans' victory over the Persians took place in the year of the Pledge of Ridwan; for this reason the reports are widespread. It was after the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf on the day of Uhud.
The reports agree that the Romans' victory over the Persians occurred after seven years had passed from the Persians' victory over the Romans, at the time when this surah was revealed. Whoever said that this was after nine years, with the letter ta' placed first, has been understood as a copying error, as related by al-Qurtubi from al-Qushayri. This implies that the revelation of Surat al-Rum was in the eleventh year before the Hijra, because the Pledge of Ridwan was in the sixth year after the Hijra. From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: the Romans' victory over Persia coincided in its day with the day of Badr.

The number of its verses according to the count of the people of Medina and the people of Mecca is fifty-nine. According to the count of the people of Syria, Basra and Kufa it is sixty.

The cause of its revelation is what al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Wahidi and others, that when the Persians and the Romans fought the war that we will mention at His saying ﴿The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land﴾ [al-Rum: 2], and the Persians overcame the Romans, the polytheists of Mecca rejoiced at the Persians' victory over the Romans, because the Persians were polytheists and were not People of the Book, so their state was closer to the state of Quraysh. Also, the Arabs of the Hijaz and Iraq were supporters of the Persians, while the Arabs of Syria were supporters of the Romans. So Quraysh showed arrogance toward the Muslims because of this. Allah revealed this surah as a rebuke to them and a refutation of their arrogance, declaring that Allah would give victory to the Romans over the Persians after some years. Therefore, when the first verses of this surah were revealed, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq went out shouting in the outskirts of Mecca: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ [al-Rum: 1], ﴿The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome﴾ [al-Rum: 2], ﴿within a few years﴾ [al-Rum: 4]. Abu Bakr made a wager with the polytheists on this, as will come.

* * *
Aims of this surah

The first aim of this surah is its cause of revelation, which was the matter that pleased the polytheists, namely the Persians' domination over the Romans. Allah suppressed the polytheists' arrogance concerning it and challenged them that the outcome would be for the Romans in overcoming the Persians after a few years.

[Page 41]
Then from this he moved on to show the ignorance of the polytheists, in that their understandings do not penetrate into reflection on events, nor into the causes of the rise and decline of nations from the divine side. Among this is their neglect of considering the second life, and they did not take warning from the destruction of earlier nations similar to them in associating others with Allah. From this he moved on to mention the resurrection.

He argued for this, and for His oneness, with proofs from the signs of Allah in the ordering of the world and the ordering of human life.

Then he urged the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims to hold fast to this religion and praised it.

He compared the virtues to which Islam calls with the state and vices of the polytheists, and he gave examples of the revival of various dead things after life has left them, and of the revival of nations after people have despaired of them, and examples of strength arising after weakness and the reverse of that.

He concluded this by returning to the establishment of the resurrection, then by strengthening the Prophet (ﷺ) and promising him victory.

Among the most important things it contains is the declaration that Islam is the religion upon which Allah created people, and that whoever seeks another religion has tried to alter what Allah created, and how could he do that?
